weaknesses: Case by case can slowly become never, especially with people who push.
realLife: On a first date: You tell them you need to leave by 10. At 10:40 you’re still there, by choice.
In a fight: You hold your line for a while, then soften the moment they look hurt.
tips: Pick your three non-negotiables and say them early. Then bend freely on the rest.
match: Best with: Someone who respects your no the first time, so you don’t have to repeat it.
Green flag: They ask before they assume, about your time, your space and your plans.
Careful with: Someone who goes cold when you set a limit, until you take it back.

tests.title: Empathy Words
tests.subtitle: How supportive your language is
tests.description: Measures how empathetic and comforting your words are (especially during stress).
tests.whatYouLearn: Your supportive language habits.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Empathy language reduces conflict and strengthens bond during hard times.

questions.text: They didn’t get the job they’d been dreaming about. They call you. Your first words:

options.text: “There’ll be better ones, don’t worry”
“Oh no. I’m so sorry. Want me to come over?”
“Their loss. Let’s fix your CV tonight”
“That sucks. What did they say?”

questions.text: Their grandmother is in hospital. They text “Can’t talk, just stressed.” You reply…

options.text: “Okay, take care”
“I’m here. No need to reply. Thinking of you all ❤️”
“Don’t worry, she’ll be fine”
“Which hospital? I know a doctor there”

questions.text: Someone starts crying in front of you. You…

options.text: Sit closer and let them cry
Freeze, then go get water

questions.text: They’re upset their closest friend forgot their birthday. You think it’s minor. You say…

options.text: “Did you remind them, though?”
“That really hurts, especially from them.”
“Let’s do something fun tonight instead!”
“It’s just a birthday. They’re busy.”

questions.text: They sigh: “I’m just so tired of everything at work.” You…

options.text: List three ways to fix it
Ask if they want advice or just to vent
Say “That sounds exhausting. Tell me.”
Say “Everyone’s job is like that”

questions.text: The night before a big presentation, they say “I’m going to mess it up.” You…

options.text: “Relax, it’s just one presentation”
“You’ll be fine, you always are!”
“Then let’s run it once more tonight”
“You’ve prepared so much. I’m proud either way.”

questions.text: They tell you their parents are fighting at home again. You…

options.text: Go quiet. You don’t know what to say
Share a story about your own parents
Say “That must be so hard to be around”
Tell them it’s time to move out

questions.text: At dinner they’re smiling, but quieter than usual. You…

options.text: Tell a funny story to lift the mood
Don’t notice until they say something
Ask softly: “You seem far away. All okay?”

tests.measures: how supportive and comforting your language is during emotional moments

VeryHigh.label: The Right Words
summaries: You always know what to say when it hurts.

You have a rare gift: when someone is falling apart, you find words that hold them together. You don’t rush their tears, you don’t say “don’t worry”, and you never make it about you. People remember what you said on their worst day, sometimes for years.
behaviors: You say “that would hurt anyone” before anything else.
Your reassurance sounds real because it’s specific: what they did, and why you’re proud.
You can sit in silence with them, and it feels like comfort, not awkwardness.
strengths: Your words heal. People feel less alone the moment you speak.
weaknesses: You give so much comfort that people forget you need it too.
realLife: On a first date: They admit they’re nervous. You say “me too, it’s nice” and the whole evening relaxes.
In a fight: Even upset, you say “I know you didn’t mean to hurt me.” Half the fight ends right there.
tips: Use your gift on yourself too. Talk to yourself the way you’d talk to them on their worst day.
match: Best with: Someone who values softness and learns your way of caring.
Green flag: They ask “how are you, really?” on your hard days.
Careful with: Someone who leans on your comfort and never asks about you.

High.label: The Shoulder to Lean On
summaries: People cry on you and leave feeling lighter.

You know most people don’t need a solution first; they need to feel understood. So you slow down, say the kind thing, and offer help only when they’re ready. When someone’s smile looks different, you notice and ask about it gently.
behaviors: You text “I’m here, no need to reply” when they’re going through it.
You ask “advice or just a listener?” and respect the answer.
You notice the quiet behind their smile at dinner.
strengths: People feel safe being sad around you.
weaknesses: You carry other people’s hurt home and sometimes forget to put it down.
realLife: On a first date: They mention their dad’s health and you put down your fork to really listen.
In a fight: You say “I can see why that hurt you,” even when your side of the story is different.
tips: Let someone hold you up too. Comfort is a two-way road, even for the strong one.
match: Best with: Someone open about feelings who comforts you back just as warmly.
Green flag: They notice when you’re the one who needs comforting.
Careful with: Someone who only shows up when they need a shoulder.

Moderate.label: The Hug-Then-Plan
summaries: A little comfort, then straight on to what’s next.

You give comfort and you give advice, in that order, just with a short gap between them. You notice when someone’s low and you care, but sitting in sadness for long makes you restless, so you move to solutions sooner than they might want.
behaviors: You say “I’m sorry, that’s rough” and then “okay, so what now?”
On a good day, you ask whether they want advice or a good rant.
You notice they’re quiet, but wait for them to bring it up.
strengths: Balance. People get both comfort and help from you.
weaknesses: The gap between the hug and the plan can be a little too short.
realLife: On a first date: They share a family worry. You listen, say something kind, then suggest a good doctor. Both help.
In a fight: You say “I get it,” then explain why they shouldn’t feel that way. Stop after the first part.
tips: Stay in the comfort part one minute longer than feels natural. That minute is where people feel loved.
match: Best with: Someone who likes a mix of comfort and practical help.
Green flag: They tell you when they’re ready to move from feeling to fixing.
Careful with: Someone who wants endless comfort and never any next step.

Low.label: The Chin-Up Coach
summaries: “Don’t worry, it’ll be fine.” Every single time.

You want the people you love to feel better fast, so you reach for perspective: it’s not that bad, everyone goes through it, there’ll be better jobs. You mean it kindly. But sometimes the hurt needs a minute before the pep talk, and you skip ahead.
behaviors: You say “it’s just one presentation” to calm their nerves.
You cheer them up by changing the plan, the topic or the mood.
You’re great at the bright side, less at sitting on the dark side with them.
strengths: You bring hope into a gloomy room. People feel lighter around you.
weaknesses: “Don’t worry” can sound like “don’t feel”, even when you mean the opposite.
realLife: On a first date: They mention a rough year. You say “but look how far you’ve come!” and they smile.
In a fight: You say “it’s not a big deal,” and it becomes a bigger deal.
tips: Swap “don’t worry” for “of course you’re worried.” Then cheer them on. The order changes everything.
match: Best with: Someone resilient who enjoys your optimism and tells you when they need a slower moment.
Green flag: They can say “I just need to be sad for a bit” without making you feel wrong.
Careful with: Someone who expects you to fix every mood, every time.

VeryLow.label: The Fix-It Brain
summaries: You show love with solutions, not soft words.

When someone you love is hurting, your brain goes straight to fixing it: a plan, a contact, a better CV by tonight. Soft words feel awkward and a bit useless to you, because what good is “I’m sorry” if nothing changes? Your care is real; it just speaks in actions.
behaviors: They’re upset about a bad day and you’re already googling solutions.
You’d rather drive across the city with medicine than find the right words on the phone.
Tears make you freeze, so you offer water, tissues and a plan.
strengths: In a real crisis, you’re the calmest, most useful person in the room.
weaknesses: Sometimes they don’t want it fixed yet. They want to feel less alone first.
realLife: On a first date: They mention a work problem. By dessert, you’ve drafted their email for them.
In a fight: You present the logical fix. They need to hear “I get why you’re upset” first.
tips: Before any fix, say one line: “That sounds really hard.” Then ask: “Do you want ideas, or just me?”
match: Best with: Someone who values a practical helper and says “just hug me” when that’s what they need.
Green flag: They tell you plainly what kind of support they want.
Careful with: Someone who calls you cold because you didn’t find the ‘right’ words.

Undecided.label: The Hug-Then-Plan

You give comfort and you give advice, in that order, just with a short gap between them. You notice when someone’s low and you care, but sitting in sadness for long makes you restless, so you move to solutions sooner than they might want.

On a good day, you ask whether they want advice or a good rant.
You notice they’re quiet, but wait for them to bring it up.

weaknesses: The gap between the hug and the plan can be a little too short.
realLife: On a first date: They share a family worry. You listen, say something kind, then suggest a good doctor. Both help.
In a fight: You say “I get it,” then explain why they shouldn’t feel that way. Stop after the first part.
tips: Stay in the comfort part one minute longer than feels natural. That minute is where people feel loved.
match: Best with: Someone who likes a mix of comfort and practical help.
Green flag: They tell you when they’re ready to move from feeling to fixing.
Careful with: Someone who wants endless comfort and never any next step.

tests.title: Repair Language
tests.subtitle: How you reconnect after tension
tests.description: Measures how you repair after tension (apologies, affection, talking, space).
tests.whatYouLearn: Your default repair style after conflict.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Helps partners repair faster instead of repeating cycles.

questions.text: Morning after a fight. You’re still a bit upset. You…

options.text: Act normal and hope it’s forgotten
Say “good morning” and see how they reply
Make them chai and say “Truce?”
Stay cool until they come to you

questions.text: After a fight, saying sorry is…

options.text: Hard. It feels like losing
Easy. I go first, even if we were both wrong

questions.text: They apologise properly for the fight. You’re still a little hurt. You…

options.text: Say “it’s fine” but bring it up next fight
Hug them: “Thank you for saying that.”
Say thanks, and that you need a bit of time
Say “okay” and stay cool for a day

questions.text: Your usual way of saying “we’re okay” after tension:

options.text: A meme, as if nothing happened
Nothing. Time does the work
A hug, a joke, and “sorry for my part”

questions.text: You snapped at your mum on the phone yesterday. Today you…

options.text: Wait for her to call. She always does
Call about something else and be extra sweet
Send a photo of your lunch, no words
Call: “Sorry, Ma. I was stressed.”

questions.text: You and an old friend fell out months ago over something silly. It’s their birthday. You…

options.text: Like their story and leave it there
Text “Happy birthday. I miss you. Sorry about that fight.”
Nothing. They should text first
Send a plain “happy birthday”

questions.text: A tense week, you’ve barely talked. It’s Friday night. You…

options.text: Plan separate weekends. Space will help
Stay busy. If they want to talk, they’ll say
Say “I’ve missed us. Dinner, no phones?”
Watch a show together, still not talking about it

questions.text: Something they said last month still stings. You…

options.text: Tell them, so you can finally let it go
Keep it, in case it’s needed later

tests.measures: how you reconnect and restore the relationship after tension

VeryHigh.label: The Make-Up Artist
summaries: You build the way back, even while you’re still hurt.

You believe love is measured by how it recovers, not by how rarely it fights. So you reach out first, say sorry without bargaining, forgive when the effort is real, and name the distance before it grows. People feel safe fighting with you because they know the way back.
behaviors: After a distant week, you say “I’ve missed us. Dinner, no phones?”
Months after a silly fight, you text “I miss you, sorry about that.”
You bring up old hurts so you can actually let them go.
strengths: No distance lasts long around you. You always find the way back.
weaknesses: You can end up doing all the repair work and forget to ask them to meet you halfway.
realLife: On a first date: A small mix-up over the bill. You laugh, sort it out, and offer to get the next one.
In a fight: Even mid-fight you say “we’re okay, we just need to sort this.” It changes the air.
tips: Let them build a bridge too. Waiting a little shows you how much they want to come back.
match: Best with: Someone who walks across the bridges you build, and builds some too.
Green flag: They reach out first sometimes, so it isn’t always you.
Careful with: Someone who waits for you to fix every fight, every time.

High.label: The Peace Offering
summaries: Chai, a hug, a sorry. You’re back by morning.

You don’t like distance, so you reach out soon after a fight, often with chai and a hug. You say sorry for your part without feeling small, and you accept theirs warmly. Being close matters more to you than being right.
behaviors: You make them chai the morning after and say “truce?”
You say “sorry for my part” even when you think they started it.
When they apologise, you hug them and mean it.
strengths: Tension never moves in with you. It visits, and then it leaves.
weaknesses: You may rush to make up before the real issue is sorted.
realLife: On a first date: You’re late, so you arrive with their favourite samosa as an apology. Point won.
In a fight: You reach for their hand while you’re still a bit upset. It softens you both.
tips: Make sure the problem gets fixed, not only the mood. A quick truce is great; a real talk after it is better.
match: Best with: Someone who accepts a peace offering and offers one back.
Green flag: They take your sorry warmly and give one of their own.
Careful with: Someone who uses your quick apologies so they never have to make one.

Moderate.label: The Meme Mender
summaries: You make up with a meme. The sorry comes later.

You do come back after a fight, usually with something light: a joke, a meme, their favourite snack. A proper talk or a full sorry takes you longer, and sometimes needs them to open the door. You get there, just by the scenic route.
behaviors: Your first move after a fight is a meme that really means “are we okay?”
You accept a sorry, but your warmth takes a day to come back.
You apologise more easily over text than face to face.
strengths: Humour. You can melt tension that others would let set.
weaknesses: A meme can paper over a hurt that still needs a real talk.
realLife: On a first date: A heated debate about a film. You end it with a joke and “rematch next week?”
In a fight: An hour later you send a funny reel. It works, mostly.
tips: After the meme, say one real line: “Sorry for my part.” The laugh opens the door; the words close the gap.
match: Best with: Someone who laughs at your peace offerings and still gets the real talk in.
Green flag: They laugh at the meme, then say “but let’s talk about it too”.
Careful with: Someone who refuses every light gesture until you grovel.

Low.label: The Act-Normal Type
summaries: Fight last night? What fight? Pass the chutney.

You don’t hold grudges; you just skip the awkward part. After tension you act like nothing happened and hope normal life covers it. Often it works, but whatever caused the fight is still there, quietly waiting for its next turn.
behaviors: The morning after a fight, your “good morning” sounds like any other day’s.
Repair talks feel so awkward that you’d rather just move on.
Sometimes you say “it’s fine” when it isn’t yet, and hope it will be.
strengths: You never let a fight ruin a whole day. Life goes on around you.
weaknesses: Skipping the sorry can leave them feeling the hurt was never noticed.
realLife: On a first date: A weird silence after a bad joke. You change the topic so smoothly they forget it happened.
In a fight: The next day you bring snacks and act like it never happened. Add one sorry line too.
tips: Add one sentence before acting normal: “Sorry about last night, I hate fighting with you.” Then pass the chutney.
match: Best with: Someone easygoing who doesn’t need long talks, but will say when one is needed.
Green flag: They keep repair talks short and kind, so you don’t dread them.
Careful with: Someone who wants a three-hour post-mortem after every small fight.

VeryLow.label: The Proud Fortress
summaries: Walls go up fast. They come down slowly.

When you’re hurt, up goes the drawbridge. You need time, distance, and usually for them to come to you first, because reaching out while you’re still sore feels like losing. Behind the walls you care a lot; you just guard that part fiercely.
behaviors: After a fight, you can go a day or two in polite silence.
You wait for them to text first, even when you miss them.
Old hurts stay with you, and sometimes reappear in new fights.
strengths: You don’t fake being okay. When you come back, you mean it.
weaknesses: The longer the wall stays up, the harder it is for anyone to knock.
realLife: On a first date: They make a careless joke about your city. You laugh, and you still remember it on date three.
In a fight: You go silent and wait for them to come to you. Inside, you’re hoping they will.
tips: Try a tiny bridge: a “hey”, or chai on their desk. You don’t have to be over it to start coming back.
match: Best with: Someone patient and warm who reaches out first without making you feel small.
Green flag: They make the first move after a fight and don’t rub it in.
Careful with: Someone just as proud. Two fortresses can stay silent for weeks.

Undecided.label: The Meme Mender

You do come back after a fight, usually with something light: a joke, a meme, their favourite snack. A proper talk or a full sorry takes you longer, and sometimes needs them to open the door. You get there, just by the scenic route.

You accept a sorry, but your warmth takes a day to come back.
You apologise more easily over text than face to face.

weaknesses: A meme can paper over a hurt that still needs a real talk.
realLife: On a first date: A heated debate about a film. You end it with a joke and “rematch next week?”
In a fight: An hour later you send a funny reel. It works, mostly.
tips: After the meme, say one real line: “Sorry for my part.” The laugh opens the door; the words close the gap.

Green flag: They laugh at the meme, then say “but let’s talk about it too”.
Careful with: Someone who refuses every light gesture until you grovel.

tests.title: Honesty & Softness
tests.subtitle: Truth without harshness
tests.description: Measures your ability to tell the truth without cruelty, and handle truth without defensiveness.
tests.whatYouLearn: How you balance honesty with kindness.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Prevents ‘truth as weapon’ dynamic and improves emotional safety.

questions.text: Before a wedding, they ask “How do I look?” Honestly, the outfit isn’t working. You say…

options.text: “Gorgeous!” Even though it isn’t
“The blue one is so you. Want to try it?”
“Change. That colour does nothing for you.”
“Not your best, but you always look good”

options.text: Ask questions until they spot it themselves
“Love it!” You don’t want to kill the dream
Say what you like, then “one thing worries me”
Point out every problem, in order

questions.text: Three dates in, you’re just not feeling it. They’re keen. You…

options.text: Say “I’m just really busy these days”
Text “Not feeling it. All the best.”
Reply less and less until it fades
Tell them: “I’ve loved this, but I don’t feel a spark”

questions.text: When the truth might hurt, you usually…

options.text: Say it straight, or not at all
Find a kind way to say it

questions.text: Your dad proudly shares a WhatsApp forward that’s clearly fake. You…

options.text: Post the fact-check in the family group
Laugh: “Papa, falling for these again?”
Call him and gently say it’s fake
Reply with a 👍 and move on

questions.text: You forgot to pay the electricity bill you said you’d handle. They ask. You…

options.text: “The app wasn’t working”
Pay it quietly and say “all done”
“I forgot, but you could’ve reminded me”
“I completely forgot. My bad, paying it now.”

questions.text: Your closest friend’s new partner was rude to the waiter. Later your friend asks what you think. You…

options.text: “They seem nice!”
Say you need more time with them first
“They seem fun, but the waiter thing bothered me”
“Honestly? Rude. You can do better.”

questions.text: They gift you a shirt you really don’t like and ask if you love it. You…

options.text: “Not my style, but thanks”
“Love it!” and leave it in the cupboard forever
“I love that you picked it for me. Can I swap the colour?”

tests.measures: how you balance truth-telling with kindness

VeryHigh.label: The Kind Mirror
summaries: People come to you for the truth, and leave feeling cared for.

You’ve learned something rare: truth and kindness aren’t opposites. You tell people what they need to hear in a way they can actually take in, and you admit your own mistakes just as easily. People trust you because you’ll never flatter them or crush them.
behaviors: You point out the hole in their plan after naming everything good in it.
You never ghost. You say “I don’t feel it” warmly and wish them well.
Your “you look amazing” is believed, because you’d say so if it wasn’t true.
strengths: You’re the one everyone asks for an honest opinion.
weaknesses: Not everyone wants a mirror every day. Sometimes they just want a cheerleader.
realLife: On a first date: You admit you were nervous and that you’re having fun. It’s honest, and it’s charming.
In a fight: You say the true thing kindly, and admit your part before they have to point it out.
tips: Ask “do you want my honest take, or just support?” Sometimes the kindest truth waits until they’re ready.
match: Best with: Someone secure who wants the real you and the real truth.
Green flag: They ask for your honest view, then actually use it.
Careful with: Someone who asks for honesty and then sulks when they get it.

High.label: The Velvet Truth
summaries: You tell the truth, and people say thank you.

You believe people deserve the truth, and that they deserve it said kindly. So you lead with something real and warm, then say the hard part clearly. You own your mistakes without excuses, which makes your honesty about others easier to hear.
behaviors: You say “the blue one is so you” instead of “not that one”.
You end things kindly and clearly, never by fading out.
You say “my bad, I forgot” without a story attached.
strengths: People trust your compliments, because they know you’d tell them otherwise.
weaknesses: Finding the kind words takes time. Sometimes the moment passes.
realLife: On a first date: They ask if you’re enjoying the evening. You say yes, and tell them exactly which part you liked best.
In a fight: You say “that hurt me” in a calm voice, with no extra digs.
tips: When the kind words won’t come, say the true ones simply. Your warmth shows even when your phrasing isn’t perfect.
match: Best with: Someone who values honesty and gives it back just as gently.
Green flag: They tell you the truth kindly, even when a white lie would be easier.
Careful with: Someone who calls cruelty “just being honest”.

Moderate.label: The Diplomat
summaries: Honest, mostly. Nicely wrapped, always.

You do tell the truth, with plenty of padding around it. You pick your words, your timing and your audience, and you’d rather say less than say it badly. People feel safe with you, though sometimes they have to read between your polite lines.
behaviors: You say “not your best look, but you always look good”.
You give your honest opinion once you’ve found the nicest way to put it.
Hard truths do come out, just a day or two later than they could.
strengths: Tact. People can hear hard things from you without getting defensive.
weaknesses: So much padding that the actual point gets lost inside it.
realLife: On a first date: The food is average. You say “interesting place!” and they laugh, because they get it.
In a fight: You say it nicely, so nicely that they miss how upset you are.
tips: Keep the kindness, trim the padding. One warm line, then the truth in one clear sentence.
match: Best with: Someone who reads between the lines, or kindly asks you to say it plainly.
Green flag: They ask “what do you really think?” and wait for it.
Careful with: Someone who takes your politeness as full approval.

Low.label: The Truth Juggler
summaries: Truth in one hand, feelings in the other. Oops.

You try to be honest and kind at the same time, and it’s a tricky juggle. Some days you soften the truth until it isn’t quite true; other days you say it straight and only see the sting afterwards. You care about both. You’re still finding the grip.
behaviors: You say “I’m just busy these days” when the truth is you’re not feeling it.
You tell them their plan has problems, all twelve of them, in order.
Owning a mistake comes with a small “but you could have reminded me”.
strengths: You care about honesty and feelings both, which is the hardest and best mix.
weaknesses: Half-truths and over-truths both make it hard for people to trust your words.
realLife: On a first date: They ask about your last relationship. You give a very edited version, then overshare on date two.
In a fight: You say “I’m fine”, and an hour later “actually, you were rude to me”, with interest.
tips: Before a hard truth, ask: is it true, is it kind, is it needed now? If one answer is no, rephrase it first.
match: Best with: Someone patient who tells you kindly how your words landed, so you can adjust.
Green flag: They thank you for honesty, even when it came out a bit clumsy.
Careful with: Someone who only ever wants to hear nice things.

VeryLow.label: The Sugar-or-Salt
summaries: Sweet fibs or salty truths, rarely both at once.

For you, honesty and kindness feel like a choice: protect their feelings or tell them the truth. So sometimes you say “love it!” about things you don’t, and sometimes the truth comes out so raw it stings. Both come from caring, just in different directions.
behaviors: You call the outfit gorgeous, then admit a month later that it was “a bit much”.
When you finally say the hard thing, it comes out all at once, with no cushion.
Fading out feels kinder to you than saying “I’m not feeling it”.
strengths: You never say hard things lightly. When you speak up, it matters.
weaknesses: Kind fibs and harsh truths both leave people unsure what you really think.
realLife: On a first date: They ask if you like the place. You say “love it” while quietly hating the music.
In a fight: You hold back all evening, then say the one line that really stings.
tips: Try the middle sentence: one kind true thing, then the hard true thing. “I love that you tried. This one isn’t working.”
match: Best with: Someone who asks for the truth gently and stays calm when they get it.
Green flag: They say “you can tell me, I won’t be upset”, and keep that promise.
Careful with: Someone who punishes honesty, so you learn to fib even more.

Undecided.label: The Diplomat
summaries: Honest, mostly. Nicely wrapped, always.

You do tell the truth, with plenty of padding around it. You pick your words, your timing and your audience, and you’d rather say less than say it badly. People feel safe with you, though sometimes they have to read between your polite lines.

You give your honest opinion once you’ve found the nicest way to put it.
Hard truths do come out, just a day or two later than they could.

In a fight: You say it nicely, so nicely that they miss how upset you are.

match: Best with: Someone who reads between the lines, or kindly asks you to say it plainly.
Green flag: They ask “what do you really think?” and wait for it.
Careful with: Someone who takes your politeness as full approval.

tests.measures: how you give and receive feedback in close relationships

VeryHigh.label: The Work in Progress
summaries: Feedback is fuel. You ask for it, and you give it kindly.

You see feedback as a shortcut to becoming a better person, so you ask for it, thank people for it, and actually use it. When you give it, you talk about the problem, not the person, and you offer a way forward. Growing alongside someone sounds exciting to you, not scary.
behaviors: You suggest a “what could we each do better?” chat and bring a list about yourself.
When a close friend says you’ve been distant, you say “ouch, you’re right” and call more.
You can hear “your mum’s comments upset me” without rushing to defend her.
strengths: You grow faster than anyone around you, and you help them grow too.
weaknesses: Not everyone wants to improve everything. Sometimes they just want to be loved as they are.
realLife: On a first date: You ask “what’s something you’re working on in yourself?” and they actually answer.
In a fight: You ask “what could I have done differently?” and listen to the whole answer.
tips: Balance the notes with praise. Tell them three things you love for every one thing you’d change.
match: Best with: Someone curious about growing, who gives you honest notes and takes yours.
Green flag: They say “thanks for telling me” and mean it.
Careful with: Someone who never admits a single thing could be better.

High.label: The Feedback Sandwich
summaries: Something nice, the real point, something nice.

You know how to say what needs changing without making anyone feel small, and you can hear it back without falling apart. You ask for what you want instead of listing what’s wrong, and you treat a complaint as information, not an attack.
behaviors: You say “I’d love it if you got to know my friends” instead of “you never try”.
A funny sticky note on the bed is how you mention the wet towel.
When they say you’re on your phone too much, you say “fair” and put it away.
strengths: People actually change after talking to you, and they still like you.
weaknesses: Sometimes there’s so much bread that the filling gets missed.
realLife: On a first date: You tell them they’re funny, then that they’ve checked their phone a lot. They put it away, smiling.
In a fight: You say “I love us, and this one thing keeps hurting,” and stay calm when they push back.
tips: For big things, skip the bread now and then. Say the point first and the love right after, so it isn’t lost.
match: Best with: Someone open who takes your suggestions as care, not control.
Green flag: They give you feedback kindly too, so it goes both ways.
Careful with: Someone who hears every suggestion as an insult, however you serve it.

Moderate.label: The Sleep-On-It Type
summaries: Stung tonight, open to it by breakfast.

Feedback stings at first and you need a night to digest it, but you do come around and often act on it. You give feedback fairly when you’re calm and less fairly when you’re tired. Most of the time, people find you open and easy to talk to.
behaviors: You say “hmm, okay” and go quiet. Next morning: “You were right.”
On good days, you can ask for a change kindly.
You dread the “what could we do better?” chat, then enjoy it once you’re in.
strengths: You change. Slowly, but for real.
weaknesses: Your night of quiet sulking can feel like punishment to the one who spoke up.
realLife: On a first date: They call your favourite film overrated. You argue a bit, and over dessert admit they have a point.
In a fight: You go quiet when criticised and come back the next day, calmer and more open.
tips: Say “I need a night with this” out loud, so your silence doesn’t sound like sulking.
match: Best with: Someone patient who gives you a night and doesn’t push for an instant answer.
Green flag: They notice when you’ve changed something and say thank you.
Careful with: Someone who brings up feedback at 11 pm when you’re running on empty.

Low.label: The Quick Comeback
summaries: Feedback comes in, a reason goes straight back out.

You’re quick and sharp, so when someone points something out, your reasons are ready before they’ve finished. It isn’t that you can’t take it; you just need to explain first. And when you’re stressed, your own feedback tends to come out as criticism.
behaviors: “You’re late a lot” gets a full traffic report from Silk Board.
You hang up the wet towel yourself, again, until it turns into a big fight.
You do change, quietly, a week later, without admitting the feedback helped.
strengths: You’re never a pushover. You think about every comment, even the unfair ones.
weaknesses: Your reasons can sound like “it’s not my fault”, even when you’re about to change.
realLife: On a first date: They gently correct a cricket fact. You produce three stats to prove you were almost right.
In a fight: You defend yourself point by point. Try “you’re right about that one” just once.
tips: Count to five before the reason comes out, and start with “fair point”. You can still explain after.
match: Best with: Someone who doesn’t mind your first reaction and waits for your second one.
Green flag: They bring things up calmly and don’t make it about your character.
Careful with: Someone who argues back just as fast. You’ll never get past the reasons.

VeryLow.label: The Hedgehog
summaries: Soft inside, spikes up the second you feel criticised.

Criticism lands on you like an attack, even when it’s meant kindly, so the spikes come out: a comeback, a list of reasons, a long sulk. Underneath, you care a lot about doing things well, which is exactly why it stings. When you feel safe, you’re as soft as anyone.
behaviors: “You’re always on your phone” gets “and you’re not?” within a second.
You replay one small comment for days, getting more hurt each time.
When you’re fed up, your feedback comes out as “why are you always like this?”
strengths: You care deeply about getting things right. Nobody holds you to higher standards than you do.
weaknesses: If every comment meets spikes, people stop telling you things, and that’s lonelier.
realLife: On a first date: They tease you about your order. You defend it for five minutes, then laugh.
In a fight: One small complaint becomes a full defence, with evidence from the past six months.
tips: When feedback comes, say only “let me think about that.” Answer the next day, once the spikes are down.
match: Best with: Someone gentle who leads with what they love before what they’d change.
Green flag: They give feedback in private, kindly, and one thing at a time.
Careful with: Someone who criticises you in front of others, or keeps a list.

Undecided.label: The Sleep-On-It Type

Feedback stings at first and you need a night to digest it, but you do come around and often act on it. You give feedback fairly when you’re calm and less fairly when you’re tired. Most of the time, people find you open and easy to talk to.

On good days, you can ask for a change kindly.
You dread the “what could we do better?” chat, then enjoy it once you’re in.

tests.measures: where you stand between traditional and modern relationship values

VeryHigh.label: The Pathfinder
summaries: Your life, your rules, written with love.

You believe the best way to live is the one you choose with open eyes, not the one handed down. You respect where you come from, but you’d rather build a home from your own values than from a list of shoulds. People come to you when they need the courage to do life their way.
behaviors: You want a relationship built on choice: who you love, how you live, what you keep.
Big decisions are for the two of you, with love to everyone else.
You’d happily skip the grand rituals for a small, honest celebration.
strengths: You give people permission to be themselves, just by being yourself.
weaknesses: You can read a ritual as a rule and miss what it means to someone who keeps it.
realLife: On a first date: You’re at the new place nobody has reviewed yet, already planning a trip together.
In a fight: You say “we don’t have to do it that way.” Then ask why it matters to them.
tips: Ask why a custom matters to them before deciding it doesn’t matter to you. Half the time, there’s a grandmother in the story.
match: Best with: Someone who also wants to design their own life and loves company doing it.
Green flag: They make big choices with you, not for you.
Careful with: Someone whose plans for your life were made before they met you.

High.label: The Remixer
summaries: You keep the beat of tradition and write new lyrics.

You love the warmth of tradition but like it remixed: the festival with a new playlist, a wedding with your own vows, Sunday lunch with flatmates instead of cousins. You question customs out loud, not to reject them, but to find the ones worth keeping. Your home will feel familiar to your parents and very much yours.
behaviors: You want a relationship of equals, with room for the customs you both like.
You’ll meet the family early, on your own terms.
Your idea of romance mixes old charm with new rules.
strengths: You keep the meaning of a custom and drop the parts that don’t fit.
weaknesses: Your remixes can feel like rejection to people who love the original.
realLife: On a first date: A classic chaat place first, then a rooftop with live music.
In a fight: You ask “why do we do it this way?” Ask it softly. It lands better.
tips: Before you change a custom, ask the person who loves it what it means to them. Then remix it together.
match: Best with: Someone who enjoys tradition and isn’t afraid to edit it with you.
Green flag: They can say no to a relative kindly and keep the peace.
Careful with: Someone who expects things done a certain way because “that’s how it’s done.”

Moderate.label: The Best-of-Both
summaries: Equally at home at a sangeet and a pub quiz.

You move between old and new without making a fuss about either. Some customs you keep because they feel right, others you skip because they don’t, and you’re at peace with both. Ask if you’re traditional or modern and you’ll say, “Depends on the day, the dish and the aunty.”
behaviors: You can win over a traditional family and a modern crowd in the same week.
You choose customs one by one, by what they mean to the two of you.
You’re happy to do the rituals their family loves and add a few of your own.
strengths: You make people from very different homes feel understood.
weaknesses: Going with the flow can hide what you actually want until it’s late.
realLife: On a first date: You suggest a heritage walk that ends at a brand-new café.
In a fight: You translate between their view and yours until it sounds like one plan.
tips: Know your three non-negotiables, old or new. Flexible people get on better when their own lines are clear.
match: Best with: Someone open-minded on either side who likes building their own mix.
Green flag: They explain why a custom matters to them instead of just insisting.
Careful with: Someone who wants you to pick a side and stay there forever.

Low.label: The Heirloom Heart
summaries: You keep the old ways that matter, polished for now.

You love your traditions, but you hold them like heirlooms, not rulebooks: precious, worth keeping, open to a little polish. You’ll do the full festival morning with family and order biryani with flatmates that night. Your roots are deep, and your windows are open.
behaviors: You’d love your family’s blessing, and you’d still choose your person yourself.
You enjoy an old-fashioned courtship: effort, flowers, meeting the parents at the right time.
You’ll bend on small customs and hold firm on the ones that carry meaning.
strengths: You can sit with grandparents and flatmates and feel at home with both.
weaknesses: You may not say which customs truly matter to you until one gets skipped.
realLife: On a first date: A classic café, your best manners, and a story about your grandmother by the second chai.
In a fight: You look for the respectful middle, then quietly wait for them to find it too.
tips: Make a short list of the traditions you’d keep in any home, and share it early. It turns surprises into choices.
match: Best with: Someone who respects where you come from and brings a little of their own.
Green flag: They want to learn your family’s festival recipes, not just eat them.
Careful with: Someone who calls every tradition outdated before asking what it means.

VeryLow.label: The Flame Keeper
summaries: You carry the old flame forward, proudly.

You grew up inside rituals, recipes and family ways that held people together, and you want to carry them on. To you, tradition isn’t a cage. It’s a thread that ties you to everyone who came before, and you know exactly what kind of home you want to build.
behaviors: You want your family to know and bless the person you choose.
Festivals with you are the full thing: early mornings, new clothes, every ritual.
You take commitment seriously and expect the same respect in return.
strengths: You bring roots, rituals and a real sense of belonging into any home.
weaknesses: You can assume your way is the way before asking how they grew up.
realLife: On a first date: You arrive on time, dressed well, and somehow your mother already knows where you are.
In a fight: You ask what the elders would say. Ask what the two of you want, too.
tips: Tell them early which traditions are non-negotiable and which can bend. Clarity now saves heartache later.
match: Best with: Someone who loves tradition as much as you, or truly enjoys joining yours.
Green flag: They ask about your customs and turn up for them, happily.
Careful with: Someone who laughs at rituals that mean the world to you.

Undecided.label: The Best-of-Both
summaries: Equally at home at a sangeet and a pub quiz.

You move between old and new without making a fuss about either. Some customs you keep because they feel right, others you skip because they don’t, and you’re at peace with both. Ask if you’re traditional or modern and you’ll say, “Depends on the day, the dish and the aunty.”

You’re happy to do the rituals their family loves and add a few of your own.

In a fight: You translate between their view and yours until it sounds like one plan.
tips: Know your three non-negotiables, old or new. Flexible people get on better when their own lines are clear.

Green flag: They explain why a custom matters to them instead of just insisting.
Careful with: Someone who wants you to pick a side and stay there forever.

tests.measures: how central family is in your decisions and life priorities

VeryHigh.label: The Family Glue
summaries: You hold everyone together, and you love it.

You’re the one who remembers every birthday, settles every family argument and shows up first when anyone needs help. Family isn’t something you visit; it’s the centre your life turns around. Your love comes with a whole crowd, and you wouldn’t have it any other way.
behaviors: You’re looking for someone who wants to join a family, not just a person.
Your family’s blessing is part of choosing someone, not a formality.
Your idea of a perfect Sunday involves at least three generations.
strengths: Your loyalty to the people you love is unshakeable.
weaknesses: You might put family peace ahead of what your relationship needs.
realLife: On a first date: Your sister is texting for updates the whole time, and your mother wants a photo.
In a fight: You want peace quickly, partly because the family will notice if something is off.
tips: Protect a little time that is only for the two of you. A strong couple makes the whole family stronger.
match: Best with: Someone from a close family who sees a full house as a happy house.
Green flag: They treat your parents like their own and pitch in at family functions.
Careful with: Someone who wants to build a life far from everyone you love.

High.label: The Boomerang
summaries: However far you go, you always come back home.

Family is your base camp. You call your parents most days, you know every cousin’s news, and big decisions feel better after a talk at home. You’ve built your own life, but home is where you go to feel like yourself again.
behaviors: You want your person to love your family, and to feel loved by them.
You’ll bring someone home early once you’re serious.
Your future plans quietly include living near your parents.
strengths: You bring a warm, ready-made circle of people into your relationship.
weaknesses: Your person may feel like they’re dating your whole family.
realLife: On a first date: You mention your family three times, and you’ve already planned how to introduce them.
In a fight: You want it sorted before the next family function.
tips: Make some decisions as a couple before you take them home. Your person needs to know they come first in some rooms.
match: Best with: Someone close to their own family who enjoys a full house.
Green flag: They remember your parents’ names and your cousin’s exam results.
Careful with: Someone who sighs every time your family calls.

Moderate.label: The Two-Home Heart
summaries: One foot in your own life, one in the family’s.

You hold two homes in your heart: the one you grew up in and the one you’re building. You’ll drive four hours for a cousin’s wedding and still say no to the fifth function. Family matters to you, and so does the life you made yourself.
behaviors: You want your person and your family to like each other, without living in each other’s pockets.
You’ll ask your parents’ opinion and still make the final call as a couple.
You split festivals between two families and somehow keep everyone happy.
strengths: You keep everyone close without losing yourself.
weaknesses: Trying to please both sides can leave you tired and nobody fully happy.
realLife: On a first date: Your mother knows you’re out. She doesn’t know with whom, yet.
In a fight: You look for the plan that works for your relationship and your family.
tips: When both sides pull, decide as a couple first, then explain to family together. One voice saves a lot of tug of war.
match: Best with: Someone who loves their family and isn’t ruled by them.
Green flag: They make time for your family and protect your time together.
Careful with: Someone who wants you to choose between them and your family.

Low.label: The Sunday Caller
summaries: Your own life all week, family time on Sundays.

You run your own life and like it that way, but family is a steady line in the background. You call on Sundays, turn up for the big days and keep the small decisions to yourself. You love your people most when there’s a little distance in between.
behaviors: You want your person to get along with your family, not live by their rules.
You’ll introduce someone to your family when it’s serious, not before.
You protect couple time, even during family visits.
strengths: You stay close to family without letting them run your life.
weaknesses: You can keep family so separate that your person feels shut out of half your world.
realLife: On a first date: You mention your family once, warmly, and then talk about everything else.
In a fight: You keep family out of it, and you expect the same.
tips: Let your person into your family stories a little earlier. It tells them they’re part of the bigger picture.
match: Best with: Someone who values their own space and keeps a warm line home.
Green flag: They’re lovely with your family and protective of your time together.
Careful with: Someone who expects family events every single weekend.

VeryLow.label: The Solo Flyer
summaries: You love your family from your own nest.

You built a life that runs on your own choices, and you’re proud of it. You love your family, but you don’t need their approval for every step, and you don’t expect them to need yours. Independence isn’t coldness. It’s how you became who you are.
behaviors: You want a relationship that belongs to the two of you, not to a committee.
You’ll be warm with their family and still make the big calls as a pair.
You won’t ask anyone’s permission to love someone.
strengths: You make decisions with a clear head, free from family pressure.
weaknesses: A family-first person may read your distance as not caring.
realLife: On a first date: Nobody back home knows you’re on a date, and that’s exactly how you like it.
In a fight: You want to solve it between the two of you. No relatives, no referees.
tips: Call home a little more than feels natural. Independence and closeness can share a room, and your family will feel it.
match: Best with: Someone independent who loves their family and their freedom too.
Green flag: They make plans with you first and tell the relatives after.
Careful with: Someone whose every decision has to clear the family group chat.

Undecided.label: The Two-Home Heart
summaries: One foot in your own life, one in the family’s.

You hold two homes in your heart: the one you grew up in and the one you’re building. You’ll drive four hours for a cousin’s wedding and still say no to the fifth function. Family matters to you, and so does the life you made yourself.
behaviors: You want your person and your family to like each other, without living in each other’s pockets.
You’ll ask your parents’ opinion and still make the final call as a couple.
You split festivals between two families and somehow keep everyone happy.
strengths: You keep everyone close without losing yourself.
weaknesses: Trying to please both sides can leave you tired and nobody fully happy.
realLife: On a first date: Your mother knows you’re out. She doesn’t know with whom, yet.
In a fight: You look for the plan that works for your relationship and your family.
tips: When both sides pull, decide as a couple first, then explain to family together. One voice saves a lot of tug of war.
match: Best with: Someone who loves their family and isn’t ruled by them.
Green flag: They make time for your family and protect your time together.
Careful with: Someone who wants you to choose between them and your family.

tests.title: Spirituality
tests.subtitle: Beliefs, meaning, inner life
tests.description: Measures how important spirituality/beliefs/meaning are in your daily life and relationships.
tests.whatYouLearn: Whether belief systems and meaning are central for you.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Helps align values around purpose, rituals, and worldview.

questions.text: A rough week. What actually helps you reset?

options.text: Sleep, good food and my favourite people
A long walk alone and some silence
A prayer, or an hour somewhere sacred
Meditation, or a page in my journal

questions.text: You run into the same stranger by chance, twice in one week. You think…

options.text: It’s a sign. Life is telling me something
Coincidence. Bengaluru is smaller than it looks

questions.text: The person you’re seeing doesn’t share your beliefs, or your lack of them. It feels…

options.text: Irrelevant. It never comes up for me
Big. Faith is something I want to share
Fine, as long as they respect mine

questions.text: Festival morning. The part you love most is…

options.text: Family, food and rituals, all mixed together
The holiday, the lights, the sweets
The prayers, and what they mean

questions.text: A big decision is coming: a new job, a move. Before you decide, you…

options.text: Pray on it, or ask a spiritual guide I trust
Sleep on it and listen to my gut
Make a pros-and-cons list

questions.text: Your idea of a truly meaningful holiday:

options.text: Mountains, no network, a sky full of stars
A new city, great food, late nights
Old temples, churches and forts, for the history
A pilgrimage, or a retreat somewhere quiet

questions.text: 2 am on a terrace, someone asks: “Do you think there’s more than this?” You say…

options.text: Maybe. I keep the question open
This is it, and that makes it precious
Yes. I feel it, and it guides me

questions.text: In a home you share someday, a corner for prayer is…

options.text: A must. Every home needs one
Not something I’d think of
Lovely, if one of us wants it

tests.measures: how important spirituality or faith is in your life and relationships

VeryHigh.label: The Devoted Soul
summaries: Your faith is the heart of who you are.

Faith isn’t one part of your life; it’s the ground everything else stands on. Your prayers, your fasts and your sacred places give you strength, purpose and a deep sense of being looked after. You want a life, and a love, with room for something bigger than both of you.
behaviors: Shared faith matters to you, because it’s at the core of your days.
You picture prayers together, festivals together, a home with a sacred corner.
You’d want both families’ blessings and, above all, the blessing from above.
strengths: Your faith gives you a steadiness that carries people through hard times.
weaknesses: Someone who believes differently may feel judged, even when you mean no harm.
realLife: On a first date: You went to prayer that morning, and you’d love to know what grounds them too.
In a fight: You look for forgiveness first, because that’s what you believe in.
tips: Speak about your faith with warmth, not rules. People feel welcome in a belief they’re invited into.
match: Best with: Someone who shares your faith, or one who honours it as deeply as you do.
Green flag: They keep your fasts and festivals in mind without being reminded.
Careful with: Someone who wants you to tone your faith down to fit in.

High.label: The Inner-Light Keeper
summaries: Faith is part of your day, quiet and steady.

Your faith or inner practice is part of your everyday: a few minutes of prayer, a thank-you before meals, a calm you go back to when life gets loud. You don’t preach about it, but it shapes how you treat people. It’s the steady light you carry into everything.
behaviors: You’d love someone who prays with you, or at least respects why you do.
You look for kindness and honesty first, because that’s what your faith asks of you.
You’d want faith to have a place in the home you build.
strengths: You stay calm when life shakes, and that calms the people around you.
weaknesses: You may assume others share your sense of right and wrong, word for word.
realLife: On a first date: You say a small thank-you before you eat, and notice how they react.
In a fight: You pause, pray or breathe, and come back softer.
tips: Share what your faith means to you, not just what you do. People connect with the why.
match: Best with: Someone spiritual too, or a respectful soul who loves how grounded you are.
Green flag: They ask about your practice and sometimes join you, by choice.
Careful with: Someone who calls your faith silly, even as a joke.

Moderate.label: The Open Seeker
summaries: Searching for meaning, in your own way.

You believe there might be more to life, and you’re curious enough to keep looking. You might meditate one month, sit quietly in a temple or a church the next, and read about the universe in between. Your inner life matters to you, but it doesn’t come with a rulebook.
behaviors: You love deep talks about why we’re here, ideally on a long drive.
You’re open to their faith and curious about their rituals.
You want someone who respects your search and doesn’t rush you to an answer.
strengths: You connect with believers and sceptics without judging either.
weaknesses: Staying open can make it hard for someone to know what you really believe.
realLife: On a first date: Somehow the talk goes from favourite food to fate, and it’s the best part.
In a fight: You take a quiet walk before you talk. It helps, so tell them that’s what you’re doing.
tips: Tell them what you’re sure of, even if it’s just two things. Seekers are easier to love when they share their map.
match: Best with: A curious soul who enjoys big questions as much as small talk.
Green flag: They can talk about meaning without preaching.
Careful with: Someone who mocks your search or wants to end it for you.

Low.label: The Gentle Sceptic
summaries: Not much of a believer, always a good guest.

You don’t practise much yourself, but you respect people who do, and you’ll happily stand through a long prayer at a friend’s home. You hold an open mind and an honest doubt side by side. Big questions interest you, just not every day.
behaviors: You’re fine with someone who prays, as long as it isn’t a condition for you.
You enjoy family rituals for the togetherness more than the belief.
You’d rather talk about the values you share than the beliefs you don’t.
strengths: You make believers and non-believers equally comfortable around you.
weaknesses: You might avoid the faith conversation until it’s suddenly a big one.
realLife: On a first date: You ask about their family’s festival traditions and genuinely want the stories.
In a fight: You stay practical and calm. Ask what feels sacred to them before deciding it isn’t important.
tips: Have the belief talk early, and lightly. Knowing where you both stand saves a heavier talk later.
match: Best with: Someone easy about belief, whatever theirs is, who never makes it a test.
Green flag: They invite you to their rituals and are fine if you just watch.
Careful with: Someone who expects you to believe exactly what they believe.

VeryLow.label: The Grounded Thinker
summaries: Feet on the ground, eyes on the facts.

You make sense of life through reason, science and the people around you, and that feels complete to you. You don’t need a higher plan to be kind, honest or full of wonder. For you, meaning is something you build, one good choice at a time.
behaviors: You’ll happily join their festivals for the people and the food.
You’d rather plan your future with logic than leave it to the stars.
You respect their beliefs and hope for the same respect for yours.
strengths: You bring clear thinking and calm logic when life gets confusing.
weaknesses: Faith can look like a choice to you, when for some people it’s who they are.
realLife: On a first date: You end up debating whether aliens exist, and you both enjoy it.
In a fight: You bring facts to the table. Bring a little feeling too.
tips: Ask what their beliefs give them, not just whether they’re true. You’ll understand the person, not just the argument.
match: Best with: Someone who thinks like you, or a believer who never needs you to convert.
Green flag: They share their beliefs without needing you to share them.
Careful with: Someone who sees your lack of belief as something to fix.

Undecided.label: The Open Seeker
summaries: Searching for meaning, in your own way.

You believe there might be more to life, and you’re curious enough to keep looking. You might meditate one month, sit quietly in a temple or a church the next, and read about the universe in between. Your inner life matters to you, but it doesn’t come with a rulebook.
behaviors: You love deep talks about why we’re here, ideally on a long drive.
You’re open to their faith and curious about their rituals.
You want someone who respects your search and doesn’t rush you to an answer.
strengths: You connect with believers and sceptics without judging either.
weaknesses: Staying open can make it hard for someone to know what you really believe.
realLife: On a first date: Somehow the talk goes from favourite food to fate, and it’s the best part.
In a fight: You take a quiet walk before you talk. It helps, so tell them that’s what you’re doing.
tips: Tell them what you’re sure of, even if it’s just two things. Seekers are easier to love when they share their map.
match: Best with: A curious soul who enjoys big questions as much as small talk.
Green flag: They can talk about meaning without preaching.
Careful with: Someone who mocks your search or wants to end it for you.

tests.title: Ambition Balance
tests.subtitle: Career focus vs relationship focus
tests.description: Measures how strongly career and personal goals drive you, and how much of your energy they take.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your priorities when life gets busy.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Prevents mismatch: one wants constant time/attention, the other is in grind mode.

questions.text: 9 pm. Your manager pings: “Quick one?” You…

options.text: Help, if it really is quick
Open the laptop. This is how you get noticed
Reply politely tomorrow morning

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in five years?

options.text: Happy. The job title is a detail
Leading a team or running my own thing
Good at my work, with time for my life
A few steps up, one at a time

questions.text: A promotion with double the travel, or the same role with weekends free?

options.text: Weekends. No title is worth missing life
Promotion. Weekends can wait a few years

questions.text: A college friend quits their job to start a company. You think…

options.text: Brave. I want that someday too
Respect. I’d need a safety net first
Good for them. Not my kind of life

questions.text: Sunday evening, honestly, you’re…

options.text: Watching a show, not thinking about work
Planning Monday and clearing a few emails
Thinking about work a little, then letting it go

questions.text: The kind of person you’d love to build a life with:

options.text: Driven, but knows how to switch off
Someone who makes evenings feel like home, career or not
A go-getter chasing big goals, like me

questions.text: Festival leave: everyone’s going home, but a big launch is next week. You…

options.text: Go home, laptop in the bag just in case
Take the days fully. The launch will survive me
Stay and work. This launch is my baby
Go home a day late, after one final check

questions.text: At a party someone asks, “So, what do you do?” You…

options.text: Light up. I could talk about work for hours
Share a bit, then move on to travel and food
Give a one-liner and ask about them

tests.measures: how driven you are by goals, career, and personal achievement

VeryHigh.label: The Empire Builder
summaries: You dream big, plan bigger and rarely clock out.

You’ve always wanted more: more skills, more responsibility, more impact. Ambition isn’t pressure to you, it’s fuel, and you’re happiest when you’re building something big. The people around you start dreaming bigger too.
behaviors: You want a power couple: two people building big things side by side.
You show love by planning a future, in detail, with them in it.
You might check mail on a holiday, and you’re working on it.
strengths: Your drive is contagious, and the people near you rise with you.
weaknesses: You can treat rest, and sometimes people, as things to fit into the schedule.
realLife: On a first date: You fit it between two calls, and still remember everything they said.
In a fight: You want to fix it fast, like a problem at work. Slow down and listen first.
tips: Put the people you love on your calendar like your biggest client. Success is sweeter with someone to share it.
match: Best with: Someone with big goals of their own who loves cheering and being cheered.
Green flag: They have their own dreams and don’t feel threatened by yours.
Careful with: Someone who wants you to choose between them and your goals.

High.label: The Head-Down Achiever
summaries: Big goals, steady grind, very few announcements.

You know where you’re going and you’re working on it, mostly when nobody’s watching. Early mornings, side projects, one more course: you put in the hours because you want the life on the other side. You don’t brag about it. You just keep going.
behaviors: You want someone who understands a busy month and celebrates the wins with you.
You show love by building a future, sometimes more than by texting all day.
You’ll plan a great date, and occasionally move it for a deadline.
strengths: You turn big dreams into calendars, and calendars into results.
weaknesses: The person you’re with can feel scheduled in rather than chosen.
realLife: On a first date: You came straight from work, slightly late, with a great question ready for them.
In a fight: You go into problem-solving mode. Ask how they feel first.
tips: Block one evening a week that work can’t touch. The future you’re building needs someone in it.
match: Best with: Someone ambitious in their own way who respects the grind.
Green flag: They ask about your goals and remember your deadlines.
Careful with: Someone who makes you feel guilty for wanting more.

Moderate.label: The Steady Climber
summaries: Moving up, one sensible step at a time.

You want to grow and you’re willing to work for it, but not at any price. You’ll stay late before a big deadline and still make it to your cousin’s sangeet. Your plan has a clear direction and a few rest stops built in.
behaviors: You make room for their career and expect the same for yours.
You plan dates around deadlines, but you do plan them.
You want to build something together, at a pace you both enjoy.
strengths: You know when to push and when to log off.
weaknesses: Balancing everything can mean nothing gets your full fire.
realLife: On a first date: You’re on time, you’ve left work at work, and you ask what they’re working towards.
In a fight: You look for a plan that works for both your calendars.
tips: Pick one season a year to go all in. Steady is great, and a little sprint now and then keeps life exciting.
match: Best with: Someone with goals of their own and a life outside them.
Green flag: They talk about their plans and ask about yours.
Careful with: Someone who expects you to drop your goals to fit theirs.

Low.label: The Log-Off Legend
summaries: Good at your job, gone at six.

You do good work and you do it well, but you’ve drawn a firm line around your life. You log off on time, protect your weekends and don’t lose sleep over the next appraisal. Ambition is welcome in your life, as long as it doesn’t take over the house.
behaviors: Your evenings are for people, and the person you’re seeing gets plenty of them.
You celebrate their wins loudly, without needing to compete.
Your idea of a power couple is two people who actually have dinner together.
strengths: You show that a good career and a full life can live side by side.
weaknesses: You might go quiet when a driven person shares big plans, and they may read it as disinterest.
realLife: On a first date: A weekday, 7 pm, and you’re on time because you left office at six.
In a fight: You want to talk it through tonight, not over a calendar invite.
tips: Keep one goal you talk about out loud. It helps an ambitious person see the fire you keep quiet.
match: Best with: Someone with healthy work hours who loves a long, slow evening.
Green flag: They respect your weekends and plan things for them.
Careful with: Someone who cancels for work every single week.

VeryLow.label: The Unhurried Heart
summaries: You measure life in good days, not designations.

You’ve figured out something many people learn late: a calm, simple life is a real achievement. You work to live, not the other way round, and your evenings, weekends and people get your best self. Success, for you, looks like peace, time and a full dinner table.
behaviors: You always have time for them, and you mean it.
You don’t bring office stress to dinner.
You’d choose a slow Sunday together over any bonus.
strengths: You’re present. When you’re with someone, you’re fully there.
weaknesses: A driven person may read your calm as a lack of plans.
realLife: On a first date: No glance at your phone, no work talk, and you’re the last to leave.
In a fight: You want it settled calmly. No rush, no deadline.
tips: Share the dreams you do have, even small ones. People love knowing where your calm is headed.
match: Best with: Someone who values time and peace over titles and targets.
Green flag: They close the laptop when they’re with you.
Careful with: Someone who measures people by their salary slip.

Undecided.label: The Steady Climber
summaries: Moving up, one sensible step at a time.

You want to grow and you’re willing to work for it, but not at any price. You’ll stay late before a big deadline and still make it to your cousin’s sangeet. Your plan has a clear direction and a few rest stops built in.
behaviors: You make room for their career and expect the same for yours.
You plan dates around deadlines, but you do plan them.
You want to build something together, at a pace you both enjoy.
strengths: You know when to push and when to log off.
weaknesses: Balancing everything can mean nothing gets your full fire.
realLife: On a first date: You’re on time, you’ve left work at work, and you ask what they’re working towards.
In a fight: You look for a plan that works for both your calendars.
tips: Pick one season a year to go all in. Steady is great, and a little sprint now and then keeps life exciting.
match: Best with: Someone with goals of their own and a life outside them.
Green flag: They talk about their plans and ask about yours.
Careful with: Someone who expects you to drop your goals to fit theirs.

tests.title: Health & Lifestyle
tests.subtitle: Habits, wellness, daily rhythm
tests.description: Measures how much you value healthy habits, routine, and lifestyle alignment.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your lifestyle discipline and wellness values.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Lifestyle mismatch (sleep, food, habits) is a huge long-term friction point.

questions.text: 6 am. The alarm for your morning run goes off. You…

options.text: Snooze. Sleep is also self-care
Up and out. The run is the best part of my day

questions.text: Midnight, and Swiggy is calling your name. You…

options.text: Order, but the lighter bowl
Drink water and sleep. Kitchen closed at 8
Biryani. Life is short

questions.text: Your idea of a great first date:

options.text: A sunrise trek or a cycle ride
Dinner, dessert and a late movie
Coffee, then a long walk

questions.text: Bedtime on a weeknight:

options.text: Around midnight, depending on the show
Whenever the reels stop being funny
10:30. My sleep is sacred

questions.text: Wedding season: three functions in a week, sweets everywhere. You…

options.text: Eat everything. It’s a wedding
Stick to my routine, mehendi or not
Enjoy it, and walk it off the next morning
Pick my favourites, skip the rest

questions.text: The person you’re seeing smokes. You…

options.text: Hope they’re cutting down, and say so once
Their life, their choice
Can’t do it. It’s a dealbreaker

options.text: Bends: shorter workouts, earlier nights
Goes out the window: chai, Maggi, 2 am
Pauses. I’ll restart next Monday
Stays. The gym is how I handle stress
