You enjoy learning new things together, at a gentle pace.
You change for the relationship when it makes sense, not to win approval.
strengths: You grow without losing yourself.
weaknesses: To someone in a hurry, going slow can look like not trying.
realLife: On a first date: You both order a dish you’ve never tried, and you’re both a little brave.
In a fight: You listen, take a day and come back with one real change.
tips: Choose one thing to work on each year, and tell them. Shared goals turn growth into a team sport.
match: Best with: Someone curious and patient who grows alongside you.
Green flag: They try new things with you, without needing them to be perfect.
Careful with: Someone who wants you to change faster than feels right.

tests.title: Repair Speed
tests.subtitle: How fast you recover after fights
tests.description: Measures how quickly you calm down and reconnect after conflict.
tests.whatYouLearn: Whether you prefer quick repair or long cool-down.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Mismatched repair speed creates long tension or feeling ‘rushed’.

questions.text: 11 pm, a proper fight, nothing sorted. Time to sleep. You…

options.text: Turn to the wall. Maybe we’ll talk tomorrow
Can’t sleep on it. We talk, even if it’s 2 am
Go cold for a day or two. They’ll know why
Say “still upset, but goodnight” and sleep

questions.text: After a fight, who usually reaches out first?

options.text: Not me. Not for a while, anyway
Me, usually within the hour

questions.text: An hour after the fight, they send a silly meme and “truce? 🥺”. You…

options.text: Smile, but say “give me a little more time”
Send one back. Truce accepted
Leave it on seen. Too soon for memes

questions.text: You fought in the morning. Tonight is your cousin’s sangeet and everyone’s dancing. You…

options.text: Squeeze their hand: “we’re okay?” Then dance
Stay at opposite ends of the hall all night
Smile for photos, talk it out on the way home
Be polite but a little cool. They’ll feel it

questions.text: Day one of a Goa trip and you’ve already fought about directions. By sunset…

options.text: We’re talking, but it’s a bit stiff
Still not talking. Even the beach looks grey
We’re sharing fries and laughing about it

questions.text: You snapped at your flatmate over the dishes last night. Next morning in the kitchen you…

options.text: Keep it short and polite. It’ll pass
Make two coffees and hand one over
Clear the air: “about last night, my bad”
Wait in my room till they’ve left

questions.text: You fought over text while at work. You get home in the evening. You…

options.text: Hug first. We can talk after
Need the evening to myself before we talk
Act normal at dinner, talk properly later
Keep the chill going till they say sorry

questions.text: After a fight, how long does it stay in your head?

options.text: A few hours. A walk sorts me out
Days. It comes back in waves
Ten minutes. Then I’m hungry and over it
A full day, give or take

tests.measures: how quickly you calm down and reconnect after a conflict

VeryHigh.label: The Instant Peacemaker
summaries: You can’t sleep on a fight. You can barely eat on one.

An unsolved fight feels like a stone in your shoe, so you fix it fast, often within minutes. You let go quickly, laugh soon after, and rarely carry anything into the next day. People love how light things feel around you.
behaviors: You text “sorry, I hate fighting with you” while the fight is still warm.
Going to bed on an unfinished fight is simply not an option for you.
Ten minutes after a fight, you’re laughing at something they said.
strengths: Nothing stays heavy for long when you’re around.
weaknesses: Fixing it fast can skip the part where they feel heard.
realLife: On a first date: A small argument about which movie to see. Two minutes later you’re sharing the popcorn and teasing them.
In a fight: You want it over in minutes, and you’ll knock on the door twice to get there.
tips: Let the peace wait ten minutes. First ask “did I get what you meant?”, then ask “are we okay?”
match: Best with: Someone who also hates long silences, or tells you kindly when they need an hour.
Green flag: They tell you honestly when they’re not ready, instead of faking “all good”.
Careful with: Someone who says “fine” just to end it, so the same fight comes back next week.

High.label: The Same-Day Mender
summaries: Fights with you don’t make it to the next morning.

You don’t like a fight hanging in the air, so you mend it the same day. You cool down fast, say what needs saying and reach out first more often than not. Being close matters more to you than being right for one more hour.
behaviors: You reach out first, even when you’re the one who was hurt.
You’d rather sort it before dinner than eat in silence.
Your hug often arrives before the whole conversation does.
strengths: Tension never gets the time to grow roots around you.
weaknesses: You can hurry someone who needs more time than you to feel okay.
realLife: On a first date: The talk turns awkward over one topic. You laugh, say “okay, new topic”, and the evening is back on track.
In a fight: You say “I hate this, can we fix it?” within the hour, and you mean it.
tips: Before you reach out, ask: “Are you ready, or do you need a bit?” Your quick heart works best when it waits for theirs.
match: Best with: Someone who likes to clear the air and get back to being silly.
Green flag: They meet your reach-out halfway instead of leaving you hanging.
Careful with: Someone who takes every quick repair as proof the fight didn’t matter.

Moderate.label: The Walk-It-Off Type
summaries: A walk, a shower, a few hours, and you’re back.

You don’t pretend to be fine straight away, and you don’t drag it out either. You take a few hours to cool, usually with a walk, music or a long shower, and then you come back ready to talk. Most fights with you are over by dinner.
behaviors: You say “give me an hour”, and then you actually come back in an hour.
You can be annoyed with them and still ask if they’ve eaten.
Big fights take you longer, but small ones are done the same day.
strengths: Your cool-down has an end, so people know you’ll come back.
weaknesses: If they need longer than your few hours, you can mistake their pace for sulking.
realLife: On a first date: A mix-up over the meeting place annoys you for ten minutes. Then you’re laughing about it.
In a fight: You step out for a walk round the block and come back with “okay, let’s talk”.
tips: Tell them your rhythm early: “I need a couple of hours, then I’m back.” It turns your walk into a promise, not an exit.
match: Best with: Someone who also likes a short break and a proper talk after it.
Green flag: They let you take your walk instead of following you from room to room.
Careful with: Someone who goes cold for days and calls it “space”.

Low.label: The Overnight Cooler
summaries: Give you one night, and you come back softer.

You don’t do instant peace. You need to walk away, sleep on it and let the hot part of your mind cool. By the next day you can talk properly, and you usually see their side better than you did at midnight.
behaviors: You’d rather say “let’s talk tomorrow” than say the wrong thing tonight.
A fight can make the next morning a little quiet. You thaw over breakfast.
Fast “are we okay?” texts can make you feel rushed.
strengths: You come back to a fight with a cool head and better words.
weaknesses: Your overnight pause can feel like a long, cold wait to someone who repairs fast.
realLife: On a first date: They tease you about your music and it stings. By the next morning you’re laughing about it over text.
In a fight: You say “let me sleep on this”, and you really do come back to it the next day.
tips: Before you sleep on it, say one warm thing: “I’m upset, but we’re okay.” They’ll sleep better, and so will you.
match: Best with: Someone who can say goodnight on an unfinished fight without panicking.
Green flag: They let you sleep on it, and they’re still warm in the morning.
Careful with: Someone who needs every fight finished before midnight, no matter what.

VeryLow.label: The Snow Globe
summaries: Shake you up, and it takes a while to settle.

When something hurts you, everything inside gets shaken up, and it doesn’t settle on a schedule. You go quiet, replay it, and need real time before things are clear again. It isn’t a game: you simply can’t pretend to be fine before you are.
behaviors: After a fight, you may need a day or two before you can laugh with them again.
A quick “we’re fine, na?” text can feel like they skipped the part that hurt.
When you do come back, it’s real. You never fake a smile before that.
strengths: Your peace is never fake. When you say “we’re okay”, you are.
weaknesses: A long silence can feel like punishment to them, even when you’re only healing.
realLife: On a first date: A joke of theirs stings a little. You go quiet for a bit, and only mention it on the third date.
In a fight: You need to leave the room, and the topic, for a day. Saying “I’ll come back to this” keeps the door open.
tips: Give your silence an end time: “I need till tomorrow evening, then let’s talk.” A pause with a date feels safe. An open one feels like a wall.
match: Best with: Someone patient and steady who doesn’t panic at a quiet day.
Green flag: They give you space and still check in gently: “here when you’re ready.”
Careful with: Someone who matches your silence with more silence until nobody remembers the way back.

Undecided.label: The Walk-It-Off Type
summaries: A walk, a shower, a few hours, and you’re back.

You don’t pretend to be fine straight away, and you don’t drag it out either. You take a few hours to cool, usually with a walk, music or a long shower, and then you come back ready to talk. Most fights with you are over by dinner.
behaviors: You say “give me an hour”, and then you actually come back in an hour.
You can be annoyed with them and still ask if they’ve eaten.
Big fights take you longer, but small ones are done the same day.
strengths: Your cool-down has an end, so people know you’ll come back.
weaknesses: If they need longer than your few hours, you can mistake their pace for sulking.
realLife: On a first date: A mix-up over the meeting place annoys you for ten minutes. Then you’re laughing about it.
In a fight: You step out for a walk round the block and come back with “okay, let’s talk”.
tips: Tell them your rhythm early: “I need a couple of hours, then I’m back.” It turns your walk into a promise, not an exit.
match: Best with: Someone who also likes a short break and a proper talk after it.
Green flag: They let you take your walk instead of following you from room to room.
Careful with: Someone who goes cold for days and calls it “space”.

tests.title: Anger Expression
tests.subtitle: How you show anger
tests.description: Measures whether you express anger calmly, sharply, or suppress it until it bursts.
tests.whatYouLearn: How you express anger and what it looks like.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Helps avoid toxic escalation by predicting anger patterns early.

questions.text: They cancel your plans last minute, for the third time this month. You…

options.text: Cool off for an hour, then call
Send a long angry rant in all caps
Call and say it straight: “I’m upset. This keeps happening.”
Type “cool. whatever.” and go offline

questions.text: When you’re really angry, your voice…

options.text: Goes up before I even notice
Gets quieter and slower

questions.text: You’re driving with them and someone cuts you off in Bengaluru traffic. You…

options.text: Mutter something and let it go
Lean on the horn and say a few words
Shrug. Bengaluru will Bengaluru

questions.text: They keep putting the water bottles back in the fridge empty. It’s been weeks. You…

options.text: Make a pointed joke about it
Bang the bottles a bit louder than needed
Hold it in, then explode about everything
Mentioned it kindly in the first week

questions.text: Your manager blames you in a meeting for a mistake that wasn’t yours. You…

options.text: Correct it on the spot, voice steady
Snap back in front of everyone
Keep quiet, then rant to everyone at lunch
Ask for five minutes with them afterwards

questions.text: In an argument, how often do you say something you later wish you hadn’t?

options.text: Sometimes, and I take it back soon after
Rarely. Even angry, I pick my words
Often. My mouth is faster than my brain

questions.text: You’re upset with them, but you’re both at a friend’s birthday dinner. You…

options.text: Go quiet and stiff. Everyone can tell
Make a sharp comment at the table
Whisper “let’s talk later” and enjoy the cake
Text them angrily from across the table

questions.text: After a really angry moment, you usually feel…

options.text: Drained. I held it all in again
Okay. I said what I felt and stayed kind
Terrible. I went too far again
Lighter, but a bit embarrassed by the volume

tests.measures: how you express anger — calmly, sharply, or explosively

VeryHigh.label: The Calm Fire
summaries: You feel the heat, and still speak softly.

You don’t pretend you aren’t angry. You just never let it take the wheel. You can look someone in the eye, say “this hurt me, and here’s why” in a normal voice, and stay kind while you do it. People trust your anger because it never burns them.
behaviors: Even furious, you say what you feel in plain, steady words.
You never use volume to win a point.
They feel safe telling you hard things, because you won’t blow up.
strengths: You can be angry and safe to be around at the same time.
weaknesses: Calm can read as “not that bothered”. Let them see how much it matters.
realLife: On a first date: They make a careless comment about your job. You tell them, lightly but clearly, and they apologise. Good start.
In a fight: You say “I’m really angry, and I want to talk about it properly”, and then you do.
tips: Don’t wait until you’re perfectly calm to bring something up. A slightly shaky “I’m upset” today beats a polished talk next week.
match: Best with: Someone who values a calm talk and stays honest even when it’s hard.
Green flag: They respect your calm instead of testing it.
Careful with: Someone who only takes you seriously once you’re shouting.

High.label: The Deep-Breath Type
summaries: Angry, yes. Out of control, rarely.

You feel anger like everyone, but you’ve learnt to give it a breath before it speaks. You might step away, count, or wait till you find the right words. When you do speak, people listen, because you don’t waste your anger on volume.
behaviors: You can say “that really hurt me” without raising your voice.
You step away when you’re heated, and come back when you can talk.
You’d rather be clear than loud, even when you’re furious.
strengths: Your anger comes with words people can actually hear.
weaknesses: Your pause can look like coldness if you don’t say why you’re taking it.
realLife: On a first date: Your cab cancels twice. You breathe, book a third and arrive with a funny story instead of a mood.
In a fight: You say “give me a minute”, then come back with the clear version of what you feel.
tips: Make the breath visible: say “I’m angry, I need a minute.” Then they know your silence is a pause, not a punishment.
match: Best with: Someone who also prefers a calm talk to a loud one.
Green flag: They can hear “I’m angry” without getting defensive.
Careful with: Someone who mistakes your calm for not caring and pushes for a reaction.

Moderate.label: The Raised Eyebrow
summaries: Calm words, with a little edge you can’t quite hide.

You mostly keep your anger in check: no shouting, no scenes. But it shows in the details, a pointed “okay”, a dry joke, an eyebrow that says more than words. On a good day you name it clearly. On a tired day, the edge does the talking.
behaviors: They can always tell you’re annoyed, even when you say “I’m fine.”
Your sarcasm gets funnier the more upset you are.
Once you’ve cooled down, you can say exactly what hurt and why.
strengths: You rarely lose control, so your anger never turns into a scene.
weaknesses: A dry joke can cut deeper than you meant it to.
realLife: On a first date: They insist on a place you hate. You say “sure, sounds great” with a smile only you understand.
In a fight: Your “okay, fine” is doing a lot of work. Swap it for the real sentence underneath.
tips: When you hear yourself say “wow, okay”, stop and say the plain version: “I’m annoyed because…”. It lands softer and gets you further.
match: Best with: Someone who gets your humour and gently asks what’s under it.
Green flag: They ask “what’s really bugging you?” instead of reacting to the tone.
Careful with: Someone who matches your sarcasm until nobody is saying anything real.

Low.label: The Long Fuse
summaries: Quiet, quiet, quiet, then one big bang.

You don’t like making a fuss, so you swallow small annoyances one after another. It looks like patience, until one tiny thing sets off everything you’ve been holding. Everyone else is surprised. You aren’t: you’ve been carrying it for weeks.
behaviors: You say “it’s fine” about small things that aren’t quite fine.
When it finally comes out, it’s ten things at once, not just the one.
After the bang, you feel lighter, and a little embarrassed.
strengths: You’re patient with small stuff far longer than most people could be.
weaknesses: They can’t fix what they never knew was bothering you.
realLife: On a first date: They’re twenty minutes late and you say “no problem”. You mention it, sharply, three dates later.
In a fight: A fight about the dishes turns into a list of everything from the last two months.
tips: Light the small sparks early. Say one small thing the day it happens: “That bugged me a little.” Then there’s nothing left to go bang.
match: Best with: Someone who asks “anything on your mind?” and really wants the answer.
Green flag: They take small complaints well, so it feels safe to mention them early.
Careful with: Someone who gets defensive at the smallest feedback, so you go back to swallowing it.

VeryLow.label: The Thunderclap
summaries: Loud, fast, and over before the rain stops.

You feel everything at full volume, and anger is no different. It comes like a monsoon storm, sudden and loud, and ten minutes later it’s gone and you’re asking what’s for dinner. The trouble is, the people around you remember the thunder longer than you do.
behaviors: You never hide that you’re upset, so they always know where they stand.
Your voice rises fast in a fight, and you’re sorry just as fast.
Once the storm passes, you’re back to warm and silly as if nothing happened.
strengths: You’re honest to the bone: no silent sulking, no games.
weaknesses: Words said at full volume stay in their ears long after you’ve calmed down.
realLife: On a first date: The restaurant loses your booking and you’re furious for one full minute. Then you’re joking with the waiter.
In a fight: Your voice goes up in the first minute. Stepping out for a glass of water before you reply changes everything.
tips: When you feel the heat rising, drop your voice on purpose and say one sentence: “I’m really angry, give me five minutes.” Then take them.
match: Best with: Someone steady who doesn’t shout back, and tells you calmly when it’s too much.
Green flag: They stay calm when you’re loud and still come back to finish the talk.
Careful with: Someone who shouts back, so every storm becomes two.

Undecided.label: The Raised Eyebrow
summaries: Calm words, with a little edge you can’t quite hide.

You mostly keep your anger in check: no shouting, no scenes. But it shows in the details, a pointed “okay”, a dry joke, an eyebrow that says more than words. On a good day you name it clearly. On a tired day, the edge does the talking.
behaviors: They can always tell you’re annoyed, even when you say “I’m fine.”
Your sarcasm gets funnier the more upset you are.
Once you’ve cooled down, you can say exactly what hurt and why.
strengths: You rarely lose control, so your anger never turns into a scene.
weaknesses: A dry joke can cut deeper than you meant it to.
realLife: On a first date: They insist on a place you hate. You say “sure, sounds great” with a smile only you understand.
In a fight: Your “okay, fine” is doing a lot of work. Swap it for the real sentence underneath.
tips: When you hear yourself say “wow, okay”, stop and say the plain version: “I’m annoyed because…”. It lands softer and gets you further.
match: Best with: Someone who gets your humour and gently asks what’s under it.
Green flag: They ask “what’s really bugging you?” instead of reacting to the tone.
Careful with: Someone who matches your sarcasm until nobody is saying anything real.

tests.title: Avoid vs Engage
tests.subtitle: Do you face issues or escape
tests.description: Shows whether you face conflict and solve it, or avoid until it grows.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your instinct: fix now vs escape now.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Avoider + engager often triggers chase/withdraw cycle.

questions.text: Something they said at dinner bothered you. It’s small, but it’s stuck in your head. You…

options.text: Wait and see if it still bugs me tomorrow
Drop hints until they figure it out
Bring it up that night, gently
Let it go. Not worth the drama

questions.text: They text: “Can we talk tonight? It’s important.” Your first feeling:

options.text: Stomach drop. Suddenly I’m very busy tonight
Okay, good. Let’s sort whatever it is
Nervous, but I’ll be there

questions.text: Your flatmate hasn’t paid their share of the wifi for two months. You…

options.text: Pay it myself. Easier than asking
Drop a reminder in the flat group and hope
Ask them straight: “Hey, the wifi money?”

questions.text: They say “it’s fine” in that tone. You…

options.text: Ask: “It doesn’t sound fine. What’s up?”
Take the “fine” and move on

questions.text: Rishta talk at home again, and you’re not ready. Your parents bring it up at dinner. You…

options.text: Nod along and change the topic
Promise to talk about it properly at the weekend
Suddenly remember an urgent work call
Say calmly, “I’m not ready. Let’s talk about why”

questions.text: A year in, you’re worried about how much they spend. You…

options.text: Make jokes about their shopping and hope they get it
Plan a calm chat about money this weekend
Say nothing. Their money, their life
Wait for the right moment, which hasn’t come yet

questions.text: A fight starts. Your body wants to…

options.text: Go for a walk, then come back to it
Leave, and never quite come back to the topic
Stay and sort it, even with my heart racing

questions.text: Your college gang planned a weekend trip and forgot to ask you. It stings. You…

options.text: Act like I didn’t notice
Post a story about “real ones” and wait
Tell them it stung, lightly but honestly

tests.measures: whether you face conflict directly or try to escape it

VeryHigh.label: The Elephant Namer
summaries: An elephant in the room? You’ll say hello to it.

You can’t stand tiptoeing. If something feels off, you name it the same day, in plain words. People find it brave, sometimes a little scary, and almost always a relief. For you, an unsaid problem weighs more than any awkward talk.
behaviors: You ask “are we okay?” the minute something feels off.
You’d rather have one hard talk tonight than a weird week.
You bring up the big topics early: money, families, kids, moving cities.
strengths: Nothing grows in secret around you.
weaknesses: Not every feeling needs a talk today. Some just need a night.
realLife: On a first date: You ask the question everyone else dodges, and somehow it makes the evening better.
In a fight: You want it all on the table now. A ten-minute break would help them meet you there.
tips: Before you name the elephant, give them a choice: “I want to talk about something. Now, or after dinner?” A choice makes it easier to say yes.
match: Best with: Someone secure who doesn’t panic at “can we talk?”
Green flag: They meet your honesty with theirs, not with defensiveness.
Careful with: Someone who calls every serious talk “drama” and leaves the room.

High.label: The Straight Talker
summaries: If something’s off, you’ll say it, kindly.

You believe most problems shrink when you look at them, so you look at them. You bring things up early, ask what’s wrong when the mood shifts, and stay in the room when it gets uncomfortable. Hard talks still make you nervous. You just don’t let that stop you.
behaviors: You ask “what’s up?” when their replies suddenly get short.
You raise worries about money or family before they turn into fights.
Your heart may race in a serious talk, but you stay in it.
strengths: Problems with you get solved while they’re still small.
weaknesses: Sometimes they need a day before the talk, and you want it now.
realLife: On a first date: You ask, lightly, what they’re actually looking for. Nobody has to guess.
In a fight: You say “let’s sort this” and keep the talk going till there’s a way forward.
tips: Check the timing before you start: “Is now a good time to talk about something?” Same honesty, better landing.
match: Best with: Someone who can handle honesty and give it back.
Green flag: They stay in the conversation instead of escaping into their phone.
Careful with: Someone who goes silent for days whenever something real comes up.

Moderate.label: The Big-Stuff-Only Type
summaries: Small stuff slides. Big stuff gets said.

You don’t raise every little thing, and you don’t run from the big ones either. You quietly sort problems into “let it go” and “we need to talk”, and you’re usually right about which is which. The timing, though, is always yours.
behaviors: You let the dishes slide, but you’ll bring up how they spoke to your mother.
You need a little time before a serious talk, then you show up for it.
You can tell the difference between a bad day and a real problem.
strengths: You save your energy for the things that matter.
weaknesses: Some things that are small to you are big to them.
realLife: On a first date: They’re five minutes late: no comment. They’re rude to the waiter: you notice, and you say something.
In a fight: You ask for a day, then come back with the one thing that really matters to you.
tips: Now and then, ask: “Is there anything I’ve let slide that’s big for you?” Your filter is good. Theirs might be different.
match: Best with: Someone who tells you clearly which things matter to them.
Green flag: They respect your timing and still don’t let important talks slide forever.
Careful with: Someone who wants to discuss every small thing the minute it happens.

Low.label: The It’s-Fine Type
summaries: “It’s fine.” It’s mostly fine. It’s not fine.

You’ll face a problem when you have to, but you’d really rather not. So you wait, hint, joke about it and hope it sorts itself out. Sometimes it does. When it doesn’t, you finally say it, usually later than you wish you had.
behaviors: You wait for the “right moment” to bring something up, and it rarely comes.
You drop hints and hope they pick them up.
When you finally say it, you’re surprised how well it goes.
strengths: You don’t make mountains out of molehills.
weaknesses: Hints are easy to miss, and then you’re left feeling unheard.
realLife: On a first date: The music is too loud and you can barely hear them. You lean in for an hour instead of asking to move.
In a fight: You say “it’s fine” twice before the real thing comes out. Skip to the third sentence.
tips: Swap one hint a week for one sentence: “Can I tell you something small that bugged me?” It’s easier than it sounds.
match: Best with: Someone who notices your hints and asks, kindly, what’s up.
Green flag: They thank you when you bring something up, so the next time is easier.
Careful with: Someone who takes every “it’s fine” at face value and never asks twice.

VeryLow.label: The Quiet Exit
summaries: Hard talk incoming? You’re already out the door.

You hate the feeling of a fight in the air, so you keep the peace at almost any price. You’d rather swallow a hurt, pay the bill or change the topic than sit through an awkward talk. Underneath, you care a lot. That’s exactly why conflict feels so scary.
behaviors: You say “it’s nothing” and hope it becomes nothing.
A “we need to talk” text can ruin your whole afternoon.
You’d rather adjust quietly than ask them to change.
strengths: You’re easy to live with, and you never pick a fight over nothing.
weaknesses: Things you never say don’t disappear. They pile up quietly until they’re too big to move.
realLife: On a first date: They pick a restaurant you don’t like. You say “love it!” and order the one thing you can eat.
In a fight: You want to leave the room, or the topic. “Give me an hour, then I’ll come back” is your bridge.
tips: Pick one small thing a week and say it out loud: “That bugged me a little.” Small talks now save you from one huge one later.
match: Best with: Someone gentle who makes hard talks feel safe and short.
Green flag: They bring things up softly, with a hug and not a lecture.
Careful with: Someone who is happy never to talk about anything real, so nothing ever gets fixed.

Undecided.label: The Big-Stuff-Only Type
summaries: Small stuff slides. Big stuff gets said.

You don’t raise every little thing, and you don’t run from the big ones either. You quietly sort problems into “let it go” and “we need to talk”, and you’re usually right about which is which. The timing, though, is always yours.
behaviors: You let the dishes slide, but you’ll bring up how they spoke to your mother.
You need a little time before a serious talk, then you show up for it.
You can tell the difference between a bad day and a real problem.
strengths: You save your energy for the things that matter.
weaknesses: Some things that are small to you are big to them.

In a fight: You ask for a day, then come back with the one thing that really matters to you.

match: Best with: Someone who tells you clearly which things matter to them.
Green flag: They respect your timing and still don’t let important talks slide forever.
Careful with: Someone who wants to discuss every small thing the minute it happens.

tests.title: Blame vs Ownership
tests.subtitle: Do you take responsibility
tests.description: Measures whether you take responsibility or default to blame/defensiveness in conflict.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your responsibility reflex under stress.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Ownership is a huge predictor of stable long-term relationships.

questions.text: You’re 20 minutes late for the movie. You took ages to get ready, and the traffic was bad too. You say…

options.text: “Have you seen the traffic? Not my fault”
“Sorry, I should’ve left earlier”
“Traffic was crazy, and I was a bit slow”

questions.text: You promised to book the train tickets and forgot. Now it’s all waitlist. You…

options.text: Point out they could’ve reminded me
Apologise, then mention how busy I was
Say “that’s on me” and look for a bus
Talk about how crazy work was this week

questions.text: A close friend tells you, kindly, that you were a bit rude at the party last night. You…

options.text: “Maybe. I was tired”
“Really? Tell me what I did”
“I was joking. People are too sensitive”

questions.text: In the middle of a fight, which is harder for you to say?

options.text: “I was wrong”
“You were wrong”

questions.text: You’re cooking together and the dal burns while you’re on your phone. “You were watching it!” You…

options.text: “You could’ve checked it too!”
Laugh and order in. Nobody’s fault
“Yes, sorry, I got distracted”
“I was replying to your text, actually”

questions.text: They point out a habit: you check your phone while they’re talking. You…

options.text: “Only when you talk about office drama”
“You’re right, I do. I’ll work on it”
“You do it too, you know”
“Sometimes, maybe. When I’m stressed”

questions.text: A project you did with a colleague flops. In the review meeting, you…

options.text: Talk about what “we” can fix next time
Make sure everyone knows which part was theirs
Start with what I could have done better
Explain what was out of my control

questions.text: The fight is over. Later, alone, you think…

options.text: “Why do they always do this?”
“We both messed up a bit”
“What did I do that made it worse?”

tests.measures: whether you take responsibility or default to blame during conflict

VeryHigh.label: The Hand-Raiser
summaries: “That was me.” Said first, said simply.

You’re the first to raise your hand when something goes wrong, and you do it without drama. Being wrong doesn’t shake who you are, so you can admit it fast and move straight to fixing it. People find it disarming: fights with you rarely get far.
behaviors: You own your mistake before they’ve finished explaining it.
You never need to win a fight to feel okay.
You ask “what did I do that made this worse?” and really want the answer.
strengths: You can end most fights with three honest words.
weaknesses: You may take the blame for things that were never yours to carry.
realLife: On a first date: You forgot your wallet. You own it, laugh, and promise the next coffee is on you.
In a fight: You say “I was wrong there” in the first five minutes. Then you check whether they had a part too.
tips: Keep raising your hand, and leave room for them to raise theirs. A fight with two owners heals faster than one with a volunteer.
match: Best with: Someone who meets your honesty with theirs instead of piling on.
Green flag: They own their share too, so it doesn’t always land on you.
Careful with: Someone who lets you say sorry for everything, including what they did.

High.label: The Honest Mirror
summaries: You look at yourself first, then at the fight.

When something goes wrong, your first question is what you could have done differently. You can hear hard feedback without crumbling, and you’d rather fix your part than prove you didn’t have one. People trust you because you never rewrite what happened.
behaviors: You say “that was my fault” without a long speech around it.
You can hear “you hurt me” and stay curious instead of defensive.
You change the habit, not just the words.
strengths: Your honesty about yourself makes it safe for others to be honest too.
weaknesses: You can stay hard on yourself long after they’ve forgiven you.
realLife: On a first date: You booked the wrong time slot. You admit it, laugh, and find a café nearby instead.
In a fight: You say “I can see my part in this” early, and it calms everything down.
tips: Own your part, then stop. Don’t pick up theirs too. Fair is better than generous here.
match: Best with: Someone who owns their part as readily as you own yours.
Green flag: They say “you’re right, my bad” as easily as you do.
Careful with: Someone happy to let you carry all the blame, every time.

Moderate.label: The Fifty-Fifty Type
summaries: It takes two to fight, and you’ll say so.
You see most fights as shared, and you’re willing to carry your half. You can say “I messed up there” without falling apart, but you also expect them to look at theirs. Fair is your favourite word.
behaviors: You own your part, and then you gently point out theirs.
You like a fight to end with both people saying something true.
When you’re clearly wrong, you say so. When it’s blurry, you split it.
strengths: You keep fights fair. Nobody becomes the only villain.
weaknesses: Sometimes it really was mostly you, and splitting it down the middle stings them.
realLife: On a first date: You both got the café address wrong. You laugh and call it a team effort.
In a fight: You say “okay, I did this part, and you did that part”. Fair, but lead with yours.
tips: When it’s clearly more you than them, skip the split. A full “that was me” builds more trust than a perfectly fair fifty-fifty.
match: Best with: Someone who can also say “my bad” without being asked twice.
Green flag: They take their half without you having to pull it out of them.
Careful with: Someone who never owns any part, so your half quietly becomes the whole.

Low.label: The Yes-But Type
summaries: You’ll own it, right after the explanation.

You do see your part, you really do. It just comes wrapped in context: the stress, the traffic, what they did first. You want to be understood before you’re judged, so the reasons come out before the responsibility.
behaviors: Your sorry often has a “but” in the middle.
You need them to see why you did it before you can admit you shouldn’t have.
Give you a day, and you usually come back and own it more fully.
strengths: You see the whole picture, not just one person’s mistake.
weaknesses: To them, a reason can sound like an excuse, even when it’s true.
realLife: On a first date: You knock over a glass and say “the table’s wobbly”. Then you laugh and admit you were waving your hands.
In a fight: You open with the context. Flip it: own your part first, then give the reasons.
tips: Put the “I was wrong” first and the reason second, or leave the reason out. Same truth, but it lands like an apology, not a defence.
match: Best with: Someone patient who hears your reasons and still gently asks for your part.
Green flag: They listen to your side before they ask for your sorry.
Careful with: Someone who jumps on every reason as proof that you never take the blame.

VeryLow.label: The Defence Lawyer
summaries: Every case has a defence, and you’ve got yours ready.

You’re sharp, quick and very good at seeing what everyone else did wrong. Being wrong feels heavier to you than it does to most people, so your mind builds a case before your heart can say sorry. Under all that defence is someone who badly doesn’t want to disappoint.
behaviors: In a fight, you have an answer for every point, and three examples.
“Yes, but” comes out of your mouth before “yes” does.
Owning a mistake feels like losing, even when it would end the fight faster.
strengths: You think fast under pressure and can argue almost any case brilliantly.
weaknesses: Winning the argument can mean they slowly stop bringing things to you.
realLife: On a first date: You’re late, and the story somehow involves the traffic, your boss and the auto driver.
In a fight: You’re building your case while they’re still talking. Pause and look for the one point where they’re right.
tips: Try one sentence a week: “You’re right about that part.” Nothing after it, no “but”. Watch how fast the fight gets smaller.
match: Best with: Someone calm and secure who doesn’t need you to lose to feel heard.
Green flag: They own their mistakes easily, which makes it feel safer to own yours.
Careful with: Someone who also has to be right, so every fight goes all the way to the high court.

Undecided.label: The Fifty-Fifty Type
summaries: It takes two to fight, and you’ll say so.
You see most fights as shared, and you’re willing to carry your half. You can say “I messed up there” without falling apart, but you also expect them to look at theirs. Fair is your favourite word.
behaviors: You own your part, and then you gently point out theirs.
You like a fight to end with both people saying something true.
When you’re clearly wrong, you say so. When it’s blurry, you split it.
strengths: You keep fights fair. Nobody becomes the only villain.
weaknesses: Sometimes it really was mostly you, and splitting it down the middle stings them.
realLife: On a first date: You both got the café address wrong. You laugh and call it a team effort.
In a fight: You say “okay, I did this part, and you did that part”. Fair, but lead with yours.
tips: When it’s clearly more you than them, skip the split. A full “that was me” builds more trust than a perfectly fair fifty-fifty.
match: Best with: Someone who can also say “my bad” without being asked twice.
Green flag: They take their half without you having to pull it out of them.
Careful with: Someone who never owns any part, so your half quietly becomes the whole.

tests.title: Compromise
tests.subtitle: Flexibility under stress
tests.description: Measures how flexible you are in finding middle ground when you disagree.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your willingness to compromise without resentment.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Compatibility improves when both can compromise or respect firm boundaries.

questions.text: Saturday plans: you want a trek, they want a lazy day at home. You…

options.text: Go on the trek, with or without them
Stay home, but sulk a little
Short hike in the morning, movie day after
Trek this week, their plan next week

questions.text: Your first Diwali as a couple. Both families want you on the main day. You…

options.text: Toss a coin and go happily wherever it lands
Lunch at one home, dinner at the other
My family. Non-negotiable

questions.text: When you give in on something, it feels like…

options.text: Losing a little, honestly
Teamwork. We’re on the same side

questions.text: The AC war at night: they want 18°C, you want 24°C. Tonight it’s set to…

options.text: 24. I’m not freezing all night
Whoever’s more tired wins tonight
22, plus a blanket for me

questions.text: You get a dream job offer in Pune. They’re settled in Bengaluru. Your first thought:

options.text: Depends how big the job really is
I’m taking it. We’ll figure the rest out
Let’s sit down and look at every option together

questions.text: Your flatmate wants to get a dog. You’re not a dog person. You…

options.text: Say no. It’s my home too
Try it for a month, then decide together
Fine, but complain about it daily
Yes, with rules: no dog in my room

questions.text: At work, it’s your idea against a colleague’s, and the team is split down the middle. You…

options.text: Let the team vote, and back the winner
Push mine. I know it’s better
Merge the best parts of both

questions.text: Planning a first date, they suggest a place you’re not keen on. You…

options.text: Send my favourite place instead
Find a third place we’d both like
Go with theirs. It’s one evening

tests.measures: how flexible and willing you are to find middle ground

VeryHigh.label: The Win-Win Wizard
summaries: You don’t split the difference. You find a better plan.

You genuinely enjoy finding the plan that works for everyone. Giving a little feels like closeness to you, not loss, and you’re good at spotting what really matters to each person. Fights with you often end with a better idea than either side started with.
behaviors: You turn “my family or yours” into a plan that makes both homes happy.
You come up with the third option nobody else had thought of.
You check what matters most to them before you dig in on anything.
strengths: You find the yes that nobody else could see.
weaknesses: Always meeting halfway can leave your own wishes quietly unmet.
realLife: On a first date: They want a rooftop, you want quiet. You find a rooftop with a quiet corner.
In a fight: You stop arguing about who’s right and start sketching a plan that fits you both.
tips: Your wishes count too. Once in a while, say “this time I’d like my way”, and let them find the win-win.
match: Best with: Someone who brings their own ideas to the table, not just their side.
Green flag: They ask what you want, and wait for a real answer.
Careful with: Someone who treats every plan like a contest they have to win.

High.label: The Happy Adjuster
summaries: Not your way, not their way: our way.

You see a difference of opinion as a puzzle you solve together, not a contest. You give easily, ask fairly, and rarely hold a grudge about who got their way. Your ego is quiet, which makes you lovely to plan anything with.
behaviors: You’re happy to take turns, and you don’t count whose turn it was.
“No problem, we’ll adjust” is practically your motto.
Both of you being happy matters more to you than winning the plan.
strengths: Plans with you work for everyone, somehow.
weaknesses: You might bend so smoothly that nobody notices what you gave up.
realLife: On a first date: They want to walk, you wanted a cab. You walk, and it turns into the best part of the evening.
In a fight: You say “okay, what if we did this?” and offer a deal that gives both of you something.
tips: Say what you want first, then bend. If you start in the middle, the middle moves toward them.
match: Best with: Someone who also gives, so the bending goes both ways.
Green flag: They notice when you’ve adjusted, and they adjust back.
Careful with: Someone who takes your flexibility as a free pass to always get their way.

Moderate.label: The Bamboo
summaries: You bend on the small stuff and stand firm on the big.

You’re easy about most things: the movie, the menu, the AC setting. But you have a few things you won’t bend on, and you know exactly what they are. That mix makes you easy to live with and hard to push around.
behaviors: You’ll happily take turns choosing the weekend plan.
On things like family time or your career, you hold your ground.
You can say “this one matters to me” and mean it.
strengths: You know which hills are worth it, and which aren’t.
weaknesses: Your list of “big things” can grow quietly when you’re stressed.
realLife: On a first date: You let them pick the café and you pick the dessert. Fair.
In a fight: You give on the small parts quickly and dig in on the one that matters. Tell them which one it is.
tips: Tell them your three non-negotiables early. Then they know everything else is open, and so do you.
match: Best with: Someone who also knows their few non-negotiables and says them early.
Green flag: They ask which things matter most to you, and they remember.
Careful with: Someone who treats every small choice like a matter of principle.

Low.label: The Hard Bargainer
summaries: You’ll meet halfway, after some serious haggling.

You’re not unbending, you just negotiate like you’re shopping at Sarojini Nagar. You give a little, ask for a lot, and want every trade to feel fair to you. You do get to a deal in the end, and you remember who gave what.
behaviors: You’ll go to their family function if they come to your office party.
You give in on small things, but you’d like it noted.
Getting stubborn when you’re upset is your weak spot, and you know it.
strengths: Your deals are clear, so nobody feels quietly cheated.
weaknesses: Love isn’t a bazaar: not every give needs a take.
realLife: On a first date: You argue cheerfully over the bill and settle on “you get coffee, I get dinner”.
In a fight: You trade point for point. Try giving one thing for free and see what happens.
tips: Once a week, give in on something without asking for anything back. It isn’t losing. It’s a gift, and they’ll feel it.
match: Best with: Someone who enjoys a bit of back-and-forth and doesn’t take it personally.
Green flag: They give without counting, which makes you want to do the same.
Careful with: Someone who haggles even harder than you, so nothing ever gets decided.

VeryLow.label: The Firm Captain
summaries: You know where the ship should go, and it goes there.

You know what you want, and you’ve usually thought it through more than anyone else. Bending feels like going against your own judgement, so you hold your ground, sometimes long after it stopped mattering. When you do give way, it means a lot, because it costs you a lot.
behaviors: You usually pick the restaurant, the route and the playlist.
Meeting halfway can feel like ending up somewhere neither of you wanted.
When you give in, you’d like it noticed, because it wasn’t easy.
strengths: You know your mind, and people never have to guess what you want.
weaknesses: If you always steer, they may stop telling you where they’d like to go.
realLife: On a first date: You suggest the place, the time and the dish they simply must try. Luckily, they love it.
In a fight: You hold your position like a fort. Try asking: “What would a version that works for both of us look like?”
tips: Before you say no, ask one question: “How much does this matter to you, out of ten?” If it’s a nine for them and a four for you, let it go.
match: Best with: Someone easygoing who says clearly when something truly matters to them.
Green flag: They push back calmly on the big things and let the small ones go.
Careful with: Someone who gives in every single time and quietly keeps a list.

Undecided.label: The Bamboo

You’re easy about most things: the movie, the menu, the AC setting. But you have a few things you won’t bend on, and you know exactly what they are. That mix makes you easy to live with and hard to push around.
behaviors: You’ll happily take turns choosing the weekend plan.
On things like family time or your career, you hold your ground.
You can say “this one matters to me” and mean it.
strengths: You know which hills are worth it, and which aren’t.
weaknesses: Your list of “big things” can grow quietly when you’re stressed.
realLife: On a first date: You let them pick the café and you pick the dessert. Fair.
In a fight: You give on the small parts quickly and dig in on the one that matters. Tell them which one it is.
tips: Tell them your three non-negotiables early. Then they know everything else is open, and so do you.
match: Best with: Someone who also knows their few non-negotiables and says them early.
Green flag: They ask which things matter most to you, and they remember.
Careful with: Someone who treats every small choice like a matter of principle.

tests.title: Fairness
tests.subtitle: Rules, respect, no cheap shots
tests.description: Measures whether you fight fair: respect, no humiliation, no cheap shots.
tests.whatYouLearn: How respectful you remain when emotions run hot.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Fair fighting prevents trauma and long-term resentment.

questions.text: Mid-fight, you know exactly what would hurt them most: a jab about their job. You…

options.text: Hint at it, then pull back
Say it. They started it
Leave it. Some things are off-limits

questions.text: In today’s fight, they bring up something from months ago. You…

options.text: Bring up something of theirs from last year
Steer back: “Let’s stick to today”
Answer it, then try to get back to today

questions.text: When you’re angry, sarcasm is…

options.text: Something I keep out of real fights
My first language, honestly

questions.text: The two of you start arguing at a family lunch. Everyone’s listening, even Nani. You…

options.text: Make a joke at their expense to win the room
Keep going, but keep it polite
Say “let’s talk about this later” and drop it
Get the family on my side

questions.text: You’ve had a big fight. Later, you tell…

options.text: The group chat, screenshots and all
Nobody. It stays between the two of us
One close person, just to vent

questions.text: You’re losing an argument about chores. Which line is most likely to come out?

options.text: “You always do this. You never help”
“Okay, fair point. Let’s figure it out”
“I’m not doing this right now”
“Wow. You sound just like your dad”

questions.text: On a lovely night, they told you a secret insecurity. Weeks later, you’re fighting. That secret…

options.text: Crosses my mind, and I bite my tongue
Slips out once. I regret it straight away
Stays locked away. It was given in trust

questions.text: Mid-argument, they roll their eyes at you. You…

options.text: Roll mine right back, harder
Give them the silent treatment for the evening
Name it calmly: “That’s not fair. Let’s talk properly”

tests.measures: whether you fight fair — no cheap shots, no humiliation, no cruelty

VeryHigh.label: The Dignity Keeper
summaries: Even mid-storm, people feel safe with you.

You’d rather lose an argument than win it by hurting someone. Even when you’re furious, you protect their dignity: no mockery, no cheap shots, no audience. People trust you with their softest stuff because they know it will never come back at them.
behaviors: You’ve never used something they told you in trust, and you never will.
When a fight starts turning nasty, you say “this isn’t us, let’s pause.”
You keep fights private, out of the group chat and away from family.
strengths: Your fights end with both people’s dignity still in one piece.
weaknesses: You may let their unfair moments slide just to keep the peace.
realLife: On a first date: They mention something tender about their family. You listen, and gently change the topic when they need it.
In a fight: Even angry, you say “I’m upset with what you did”, never “you’re the problem”.
tips: Your fairness is precious, so ask for it back: “I never bring up your past. Please don’t bring up mine.” Fair rules work both ways.
match: Best with: Someone who plays by the same rules, and notices that you do.
Green flag: They protect your soft spots the way you protect theirs.
Careful with: Someone who takes your fairness as room to be unfair.

High.label: The Straight Bat
summaries: You play it straight, even when the game gets tough.

In a fight, you stick to the issue and leave the person alone. No digs about their family, no old files, no laughing at their hurt. You might get loud or stubborn, but you never make it personal, and people can tell.
behaviors: You argue about the dishes, not about who they are.
Their secrets stay secret, even on your angriest day.
You catch yourself when you start to slip, and you change course.
strengths: People can fight with you and still feel respected.
weaknesses: You expect the same rules from them, and it shakes you when they break them.
realLife: On a first date: A debate about a film gets lively. You argue about the film, never their taste, and they love it.
In a fight: Even at your loudest, you stick to the one thing you’re fighting about.
tips: Say your rules out loud early: “In a fight, I’ll never bring up your family.” Invite them into the same rules, and they get easier to keep.
match: Best with: Someone who also keeps fights about the problem, not the person.
Green flag: They keep your weak spots safe, the way you keep theirs.
Careful with: Someone who brings up your past every time they start losing.

Moderate.label: The Oops-I-Said-It Type
summaries: Fair on most days. On the worst days, a slip.

You believe in fighting fair, and mostly you do: no insults, no dragging in the family. But when you’re really hurt, one line slips out that you’d never say calm. You know it the second it leaves your mouth, and you’re usually the first to take it back.
behaviors: You keep fights about the issue, until you’re really tired or really hurt.
Once in a while you bring up an old thing, and regret it at once.
Your apologies for a cheap line come fast and sincere.
strengths: You notice your own slips and own them quickly.
weaknesses: In their memory, one slip can outweigh ten fair fights.
realLife: On a first date: You tease them about their football team a bit too hard, see their face, and laugh it off with a sorry.
In a fight: You’re fair for twenty minutes. Then you’re tired, and the slip comes. Call a break before minute twenty.
tips: Know your slip zone: tired, hungry, late at night. Don’t fight there. “Let’s finish this after dinner” saves you a sorry.
match: Best with: Someone forgiving who tells you plainly when a line went too far.
Green flag: They accept a real apology for a slip without holding it over you.
Careful with: Someone who saves your worst line and quotes it back for months.

Low.label: The Sarcasm Artist
summaries: Quiet voice, sharp tongue.

You rarely shout, but your words can cut. When a fight heats up, the eye-roll, the “wow, okay” and the clever jab come out to play. It’s how you protect yourself, but to the other person, it can feel like being laughed at while they’re hurting.
behaviors: In a fight, you reach for a funny line before an honest one.
“Always” and “never” slip into your sentences when you’re upset.
You apologise for the tone later, even when you stand by the point.
strengths: You stay funny under pressure, and used kindly, that breaks the tension.
weaknesses: Sarcasm in a fight feels like a joke to you and like mockery to them.
realLife: On a first date: You tease them about their order. It lands well, and you know to stop right there.
In a fight: You say “wow, great” with a look. Try the plain version instead: “That hurt me.”
tips: When a clever line is coming, ask: “Will this help, or just win?” If it only wins, save it for roasting your cousins, not for a fight.
match: Best with: Someone with thick skin and a soft heart who calls out the jab with a smile.
Green flag: They tell you kindly when a joke hurt, and you listen.
Careful with: Someone who matches you jab for jab until neither of you says anything true.

VeryLow.label: The Last-Word Warrior
summaries: You fight to win, and you usually do. That’s the problem.

You’re quick, clever and you know people well, which in a fight means you know exactly where it hurts. When you feel attacked, winning becomes the whole point, and the sharpest line is out before your kinder self can stop it. It isn’t cruelty. It’s the fear of losing, and it comes out as a sting.
behaviors: You remember every old mistake, and in a fight they all come back.
Your comebacks are brilliant, and some of them hurt for days.
After the fight, the line you used bothers you, even if you won.
strengths: You’re sharp and honest. Nobody ever wonders what you think.
weaknesses: You can win the fight and lose a little of their trust each time.
realLife: On a first date: A friendly cricket debate and you go for the win, with stats. They laugh, and you remember it’s a date.
In a fight: The sharpest line is already on your tongue. Swallow it, and say the hurt underneath instead: “I feel ignored.”
tips: Make three things off-limits before you ever fight: their family, their body, their secrets. Tell them. Then keep it, every time.
match: Best with: Someone calm and secure who won’t take the bait, and tells you when you’ve crossed a line.
Green flag: They say “that wasn’t fair” calmly, instead of snapping back.
Careful with: Someone who fights just as sharp, so both of you walk away hurt.

Undecided.label: The Oops-I-Said-It Type

You believe in fighting fair, and mostly you do: no insults, no dragging in the family. But when you’re really hurt, one line slips out that you’d never say calm. You know it the second it leaves your mouth, and you’re usually the first to take it back.

Once in a while you bring up an old thing, and regret it at once.
Your apologies for a cheap line come fast and sincere.

weaknesses: In their memory, one slip can outweigh ten fair fights.

In a fight: You’re fair for twenty minutes. Then you’re tired, and the slip comes. Call a break before minute twenty.

tests.title: Escalation
tests.subtitle: How fast conflict heats up
tests.description: Measures how quickly conflict escalates for you and whether you can slow it down.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your heat-up speed and self-control.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Predicts whether fights become explosive or remain manageable.

questions.text: A tiny argument about who forgot to buy milk. Five minutes later…

options.text: We’re a bit snappy, then we laugh it off
We’re both loud, and it’s not about milk anymore
It was about milk, and it’s already over
We’re onto who does more around the house

questions.text: They raise their voice. Without thinking, you…

options.text: Match it
Lower mine

questions.text: The argument is going round in circles for the third time. You…

options.text: Push harder. This time they’ll get it
Keep at it, but slower
Call a timeout: “Let’s take ten minutes”

questions.text: Family dinner. You and an uncle get into politics, and the table goes quiet. You…

options.text: Make one last point, then drop it
Laugh, pass the dal and change the topic
Get sharper till someone steps in
Go all in. Somebody has to tell him

questions.text: They say: “I need a break. Can we pause this?” You…

options.text: “No, let’s finish this now”
“Okay, back in twenty”, and mean it
Pause, but sulk until they’re back

questions.text: A fight breaks out over WhatsApp. Your messages get…

options.text: Slower. I reread before I hit send
Longer, faster, more capital letters
Shorter, then “can I call you?”

questions.text: Mid-fight, they say something that really stings. In the next minute, you…

options.text: Go quiet and stew
Say “ouch, that hurt” without stinging back
Sting back, a little harder

questions.text: You’re arguing in a restaurant. Voices are rising and people are looking. You…

options.text: Don’t notice anyone. I’m mid-point
Whisper-fight till we’re out of there
Lower my voice: “Let’s finish this at home”

tests.measures: how quickly your conflicts heat up and whether you can de-escalate

VeryHigh.label: The Volume Knob
summaries: You turn any fight down to a talk.

You have a gift for cooling a room. When voices rise, yours drops. When someone stings, you name the hurt instead of stinging back. You still have strong feelings, but you hold them steady so the conversation can go somewhere better.
behaviors: When they snap, you say “ouch” instead of snapping back.
Even in a heated fight, you keep your voice at talking level.
Fights with you rarely make it past round one.
strengths: You can calm a storm without pretending there isn’t one.
weaknesses: Always being the calm one can leave your own feelings unsaid.
realLife: On a first date: They get worked up about a bad review of their favourite café. You laugh, ask why it matters to them, and it becomes a great story.
In a fight: You say “we’re on the same side here” in a soft voice, and the temperature drops.
tips: Teach them your trick. Share what helps you stay cool, so you’re not the only one in the house who knows where the knob is.
match: Best with: Someone who calms down when they see you calm, not the opposite.
Green flag: They take turns being the calm one, so it isn’t always you.
Careful with: Someone who reads your calm as not caring and turns up the heat to get a reaction.

High.label: The Pause Button
summaries: When it gets too hot, you’re the one who says “wait”.

You can feel a fight going wrong before it does, and you know how to stop it. You lower your voice, ask for a break or say “let’s start again”. It isn’t that you don’t feel the heat. You just care more about the person than the point.
behaviors: You say “let’s take ten minutes” and actually come back after ten.
When they get loud, you deliberately get quieter.
You move a hot text fight to a call before it spirals.
strengths: You can stop a fight before it turns into something you’ll both regret.
weaknesses: Pausing too often can feel like dodging if you don’t come back to finish.
realLife: On a first date: A debate about the best biryani in town starts getting heated. You call a truce: you’ll try both, together.
In a fight: Voices rising? You say “wait, I don’t want to fight like this” and lower yours.
tips: Always give your pause a return time: “Ten minutes, then let’s finish.” A break with an end feels safe to both of you.
match: Best with: Someone who respects a break and returns ready to talk.
Green flag: They take your pause seriously instead of chasing the fight.
Careful with: Someone who calls every pause “running away”.

Moderate.label: The Slow Simmer
summaries: You get warm, rarely boil, and you can turn it down.

Arguments warm you up, but you rarely boil over. You might get snappy or stiff, yet you can usually catch yourself, slow down or let a point go. On tired days your heat climbs higher than you’d like. On good days, you’re the one who turns it down.
behaviors: You get a bit snappy in a fight, then catch yourself and laugh it off.
You can take a break, though you may sulk a little through it.
Tiredness and hunger set you off more than the topic does.
strengths: You can feel the heat without letting it take over.
weaknesses: Your quiet stewing after a fight can keep the heat on longer than the fight did.
realLife: On a first date: They insist the first Iron Man is the best one. You argue back, warmly, then let it go with a grin.
In a fight: You’re snappy for a minute, then you say “okay, sorry, let me say that again”.
tips: Know your three sparks: tired, hungry, rushed. If two are on, say “can we do this after food?”
match: Best with: Someone who knows when to crack a joke and when to give you a minute.
Green flag: They can laugh with you in the middle of a fight.
Careful with: Someone who keeps turning the heat up while you’re trying to turn it down.

Low.label: The Whistling Kettle
summaries: Warm, then hot, then everyone hears about it.

You don’t start fights hot, but you heat up as they go. Each round gets a little louder and a little sharper, until you hear yourself and think “how did we get here?” You can cool things down once you notice. The trick is noticing sooner.
behaviors: You start calm, and somewhere around minute ten your voice rises.
Over text, your messages get longer and faster as the fight goes on.
You often need someone else to say “stop” before you do.
strengths: You stay in the conversation and never leave a fight half-said.
weaknesses: You only notice the heat once the kettle is already whistling.
realLife: On a first date: A friendly argument about pineapple on pizza gets surprisingly intense. They grin, and you hear yourself.
In a fight: Minute ten, and you’re louder. Notice it, say it out loud, and sit down.
tips: Set an inner timer: if a fight hits fifteen minutes with no progress, call a break. You don’t have to feel calm to stop.
match: Best with: Someone who calmly points out when it’s getting hot, without blame.
Green flag: They say “we’re getting loud, let’s slow down” in a kind way.
Careful with: Someone who keeps pushing after you’ve asked for a breather.

VeryLow.label: The Hot Tadka
summaries: Calm one second, crackling the next.

You go from calm to full sizzle in seconds, like mustard seeds in hot oil. You feel things big and fast, and once a fight starts, you need to see it through. The heat isn’t meanness, it’s how strongly you care, though the people around you don’t always feel it that way.
behaviors: A small thing like milk can turn into “you never help” in five minutes.
When they get louder, you get louder, almost without choosing to.
Stopping halfway feels impossible, so fights can run late into the night.
strengths: You’re passionate and real. You never fake calm.
weaknesses: Heat spreads. By the time you’ve cooled down, they may still be smarting.
realLife: On a first date: A friendly debate about the best movie of the year gets so loud the next table joins in. You laugh about it all the way home.
In a fight: Round three, voices rising. Say “timeout, ten minutes” and step away from the stove.
tips: Pick a pause word together, something silly like “tadka”. When either of you says it, you both stop for ten minutes. No questions asked.
match: Best with: Someone steady who lowers their voice when you raise yours, and asks for breaks kindly.
Green flag: They ask for a pause and actually come back to finish the talk.
Careful with: Someone who heats up as fast as you, so every small spark becomes a fire.

Undecided.label: The Slow Simmer
summaries: You get warm, rarely boil, and you can turn it down.

Arguments warm you up, but you rarely boil over. You might get snappy or stiff, yet you can usually catch yourself, slow down or let a point go. On tired days your heat climbs higher than you’d like. On good days, you’re the one who turns it down.

You can take a break, though you may sulk a little through it.
Tiredness and hunger set you off more than the topic does.

weaknesses: Your quiet stewing after a fight can keep the heat on longer than the fight did.
realLife: On a first date: They insist the first Iron Man is the best one. You argue back, warmly, then let it go with a grin.
In a fight: You’re snappy for a minute, then you say “okay, sorry, let me say that again”.
tips: Know your three sparks: tired, hungry, rushed. If two are on, say “can we do this after food?”
