Green flag: They can laugh with you in the middle of a fight.
Careful with: Someone who keeps turning the heat up while you’re trying to turn it down.

tests.title: Apology Style
tests.subtitle: How you say sorry
tests.description: Measures how sincerely you apologize and how you handle repair after mistakes.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your apology maturity and repair behavior.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Apology style predicts long-term trust and emotional safety.

questions.text: You promised to call before their big interview, and you forgot. When you realise, you…

options.text: Send a sorry, plus the reason I forgot
Text “sorry, crazy day 🙈” and move on
Call: “I’m so sorry I forgot. How did it go?”
Ask how it went and hope they didn’t notice

questions.text: Which sorry sounds most like you?

options.text: “Sorry if you felt hurt”
“I’m sorry I said that. It was unfair”
“Sorry, but you also…”
“Okay, sorry. Happy now?”

questions.text: You were mostly right in the fight, but you did say one harsh thing. You…

options.text: Wait for their sorry first. They owe me more
Apologise for the harsh thing anyway
Apologise, then remind them I was right

questions.text: When you’re wrong, saying “I’m sorry” out loud feels…

options.text: Like swallowing a brick
Easy. It’s just the truth

questions.text: You snapped at a junior at work, in front of the whole team. You…

options.text: Be extra nice to them all week instead
Nothing. Work is work
Say sorry privately, quick and quiet
Apologise in front of the same team

questions.text: You’ve apologised, but they’re still upset. You…

options.text: Say “I already said sorry, what more?”
Give them space and try again tomorrow
Ask what would help, and really listen

questions.text: You keep running late, and you’ve said sorry for it three times. The fourth time, you…

options.text: Say sorry again, and mean it
Blame the traffic again
Stop saying sorry and start leaving earlier

questions.text: “Have you eaten?” is how many parents say sorry. Your own sorry usually looks like…

options.text: Chai, food and acting normal
Clear words: “I was wrong, I’m sorry”
Honestly, it doesn’t look like much
A bit of both: a sorry and a cup of chai

tests.measures: how sincerely and effectively you apologize after mistakes

VeryHigh.label: The Sorry-and-Fix Type
summaries: Your sorry comes with a toolbox.

For you, an apology has three parts: what you did, why it hurt, and what you’ll do differently. You don’t wait to be asked, you don’t add a “but”, and you actually change the habit. People trust your sorry because they’ve seen what follows it.
behaviors: You apologise without being asked, and without a “but”.
You ask “what would make this better?” and really listen.
Late twice? Your third sorry is you, arriving ten minutes early.
strengths: Your apologies are so real that trust grows after every mistake.
weaknesses: You can over-apologise, saying sorry even for things that weren’t yours.
realLife: On a first date: You’re five minutes late. You say why in one line, apologise, and the coffee is on you.
In a fight: You stop mid-fight to say “sorry, that came out wrong”, and then you say it right.
tips: Keep your sorries for what’s really yours. If you apologise for everything, the important ones get lost.
match: Best with: Someone who also says sorry with words and with actions.
Green flag: They forgive you fully once you’ve made it right.
Careful with: Someone who keeps asking for more apologies after you’ve already fixed it.

High.label: The Honest Sorry
summaries: Clear words, real meaning, no fine print.

You say sorry plainly when you’re wrong, and you name what you did instead of hiding behind “if you felt hurt”. You don’t need to be fully wrong to apologise for your part. Pride matters to you, but people matter more.
behaviors: You say “I’m sorry I said that, it wasn’t fair”, and you stop there.
You apologise for your part even when they were mostly wrong.
You ask “are we okay?” after the sorry, not instead of it.
strengths: Your sorry ends fights instead of starting new ones.
weaknesses: You can say sorry so smoothly that they wonder if it costs you anything.
realLife: On a first date: You get their name slightly wrong in a text. You own it with a funny sorry, and they love it.
In a fight: You say “I’m sorry I raised my voice” in the middle of the fight, and the whole tone changes.
tips: After the sorry, add one small change: “Next time I’ll call before I’m late.” Words plus a change make it stick.
match: Best with: Someone who also apologises with words, not just gestures.
Green flag: They accept your sorry without making you pay for it.
Careful with: Someone who takes your easy apologies as proof that everything is your fault.

Moderate.label: The Sorry-for-Sorry Type
summaries: Happy to say sorry, as long as it’s a two-way street.

When you’re clearly wrong, you say so, no drama. When the blame is shared, though, you want the sorry to go both ways, and you can get stuck waiting for theirs. You believe in fairness, and your apologies show it, sometimes a little too exactly.
behaviors: Your sorry comes easily when it’s obviously your fault.
When you both messed up, it sounds like “sorry, but you also…”
Now and then you say sorry just to end it, and bring it up again later.
strengths: You never hand out empty apologies just to look good.
weaknesses: Waiting for their sorry first can turn one fight into a three-day standoff.
realLife: On a first date: You both mixed up the meeting place. You laugh: “Sorry, my bad. And yours.”
In a fight: You hold your sorry until they offer theirs. Go first this once, and watch what happens.
tips: Say your sorry without the “but”. Their part can be its own talk, five minutes later.
match: Best with: Someone who says their sorry easily, so yours flows too.
Green flag: They own their half without you having to point to it.
Careful with: Someone who never apologises, so you slowly stop wanting to either.

Low.label: The Biryani Apology
summaries: Why say sorry when you can send biryani?

You do feel sorry, and you show it the way many of us grew up with: food, favours and acting normal. The actual words feel awkward, so a Swiggy order or a cup of chai does the talking. It’s sweet, and it usually works, until they need to hear it said.
behaviors: After a fight, their favourite dessert reaches the door before your sorry does.
You’re extra helpful for a day instead of saying the words.
If they don’t pick up on the gesture, you feel a little hurt yourself.
strengths: Your apologies are generous. Nobody makes up with more effort.
weaknesses: Food without words can feel like the fight was skipped, not settled.
realLife: On a first date: You’re late, and you arrive with their favourite chocolate instead of an excuse. Clever.
In a fight: You want to fix it with a treat. Bring the treat, and add one sentence: “I’m sorry I said that.”
tips: Keep the biryani, just add the words: “Sorry I snapped. This is for you.” Gesture plus sentence is the full meal.
match: Best with: Someone who loves your gestures and tells you kindly when they need the words too.
Green flag: They say thank you for the biryani and still ask to talk.
Careful with: Someone who only accepts a grand apology and ignores all the small ones.

VeryLow.label: The Proud Peacock
summaries: Feathers up, sorry stuck somewhere in the throat.

You feel things deeply, but “sorry” is the hardest word in your dictionary. Saying it feels like handing over your crown, so you wait it out, act as if nothing happened, or wait for them to go first. Inside, you know when you were wrong. Getting it out of your mouth is the hard part.
behaviors: You’d rather act as if the fight never happened than say the word.
If they also messed up, you wait for their sorry first.
A forced apology from you sounds like “okay, fine, sorry, happy?”
strengths: You have real self-respect. You never grovel or fake a sorry you don’t feel.
weaknesses: Without the words, they can’t be sure you know what hurt them.
realLife: On a first date: You spill coffee on their sleeve. You hand over every napkin in the café and turn red, but the “sorry” arrives a little late.
In a fight: You know you were wrong by minute five. Saying it at minute five, not day five, is the challenge.
tips: Start with the smallest true version: “I was wrong about that part.” Six words. Your feathers will survive it.
match: Best with: Someone patient who makes saying sorry feel safe, not like losing.
Green flag: They apologise easily themselves, and never gloat when you do.
Careful with: Someone who treats your sorry as a trophy to win, so it gets even harder to say.

Undecided.label: The Sorry-for-Sorry Type
summaries: Happy to say sorry, as long as it’s a two-way street.

When you’re clearly wrong, you say so, no drama. When the blame is shared, though, you want the sorry to go both ways, and you can get stuck waiting for theirs. You believe in fairness, and your apologies show it, sometimes a little too exactly.
behaviors: Your sorry comes easily when it’s obviously your fault.
When you both messed up, it sounds like “sorry, but you also…”
Now and then you say sorry just to end it, and bring it up again later.
strengths: You never hand out empty apologies just to look good.
weaknesses: Waiting for their sorry first can turn one fight into a three-day standoff.
realLife: On a first date: You both mixed up the meeting place. You laugh: “Sorry, my bad. And yours.”
In a fight: You hold your sorry until they offer theirs. Go first this once, and watch what happens.
tips: Say your sorry without the “but”. Their part can be its own talk, five minutes later.
match: Best with: Someone who says their sorry easily, so yours flows too.
Green flag: They own their half without you having to point to it.
Careful with: Someone who never apologises, so you slowly stop wanting to either.

tests.title: Problem Solving
tests.subtitle: Solutions vs drama
tests.description: Measures whether you focus on solutions and steps, or stay stuck in emotion and blame.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your conflict skill: solve vs loop.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Solution mindset reduces repeated fights and improves compatibility long-term.

questions.text: The dishes fight, for the fifth time this month. This time you…

options.text: Talk it out again, but no plan comes of it
Have the same fight, just a little louder
Suggest a simple rule: I cook, you wash
Do them myself, quietly annoyed

questions.text: They say: “We never go out anymore. It’s always Netflix.” You…

options.text: Promise to go out more, then forget
Plan one proper date a week, starting Friday
Say “so plan something, then”, and we’re off

questions.text: In a fight, which question sounds more like you?

options.text: “Who started this?”
“What do we do now?”

questions.text: Long distance, Delhi and Pune, and you keep fighting about calls. You…

options.text: Try harder for a week, then slip back
Argue about who puts in more effort
Set a call routine we can both keep
Keep missing calls and saying sorry

questions.text: Every visit to their parents ends with the two of you fighting in the car home. You…

options.text: Fight in the car again. It’s tradition now
Vent on the drive, then forget till next time
Talk before the next visit: what sets us off?

questions.text: You and your sibling can’t settle on a plan for your parents’ anniversary. It’s been days. You…

options.text: Keep arguing in the family group
Let a cousin break the tie
List both ideas, pick the best bits, decide tonight

questions.text: A big fight is finally over. Next, you…

options.text: Hug and never mention it again
Talk about what to do differently next time
Rehash who said what, again

questions.text: Halfway through, you realise it’s the same fight as last month. You…

options.text: Sigh and drop it. This one can’t be fixed
Say “wait, same fight. What’s really going on?”
Keep going. Maybe this time we’ll sort it

tests.measures: whether you focus on finding solutions or stay stuck in emotion and blame

VeryHigh.label: The Treaty Writer
summaries: Every fight ends with a peace deal, signed.

You don’t just end fights, you end them for good. You spot the pattern, name what’s really going on, and suggest a deal you can both keep. Repeat fights bother you more than loud ones, because a problem that keeps coming back is a problem nobody has fixed yet.
behaviors: You say “wait, this is last month’s fight” and dig for the real issue.
You love a simple rule: I cook, you wash. Fight over, forever.
You check in on your deals a few weeks later to see if they’re working.
strengths: Old fights with you actually stay solved.
weaknesses: A plan can feel cold if they haven’t felt heard yet.
realLife: On a first date: You can’t pick a movie, so you suggest a system: they choose tonight, you choose next time. There’s already a next time.
In a fight: Halfway through, you ask “what do we actually want to change?”, and the fight turns into a plan.
tips: Listen first, even when the answer is obvious to you. People keep the deals they helped make, not the ones handed to them.
match: Best with: Someone who likes clear deals and keeps their side of them.
Green flag: They bring ideas to the table too, not just complaints.
Careful with: Someone who wants to talk about every fight for hours but never wants to change anything.

High.label: The Jugaad Fixer
summaries: Any problem, you’ll find a clever way round it.

You see a fight as a problem with a solution in it somewhere, and you enjoy finding it. A date night, a chore chart, a call routine: you’d rather change one small thing than have the same fight twice. You still feel things. You just like your feelings to lead somewhere.
behaviors: You turn “you never call” into a Sunday 8 pm call you both keep.
You’d rather change one small habit than win one big argument.
You notice repeat fights and look for what’s really under them.
strengths: Fights with you end with a plan, not just a truce.
weaknesses: Sometimes they need a hug before a fix, and you skip straight to the fix.
realLife: On a first date: The restaurant’s full, it’s raining and the cab is late. You find a tiny dosa place nearby, and it’s perfect.
In a fight: You say “okay, what if we try this for a week?” and, annoyingly, it works.
tips: Before you offer a fix, ask: “Do you want ideas, or do you want me to listen?” The fix lands better when they’re ready for it.
match: Best with: Someone practical who likes trying new ideas together.
Green flag: They actually keep the plans you make together.
Careful with: Someone who says yes to every plan and follows none of them.

Moderate.label: The Feel-Then-Fix Type
summaries: First the feelings, then the fixing.

You need a few minutes to let the feelings out, and then you’re ready to think. You’re good at finding a fix once the heat is gone, though the fixes don’t always stick. Some fights you solve, some you just survive, and you can tell which is which.
behaviors: You rant first, then say “okay, what do we do?”
You come up with plans that work, for a few weeks at least.
When a fight repeats, you notice it on the third round, not the first.
strengths: You can go from upset to useful in one conversation.
weaknesses: Your plans can fade once the fight does.
realLife: On a first date: The café you picked is shut. You grumble for a minute, then find a better one round the corner.
In a fight: You need five minutes of “I can’t believe this”, and then you’re the one with an idea.
tips: When you make a plan, set a check-in: “Let’s see how it’s going in two weeks.” Plans that get checked on tend to stick.
match: Best with: Someone who gives you room to vent and then helps you build a plan.
Green flag: They remember the plan you made and check in on it, kindly.
Careful with: Someone who wants a solution before you’ve finished being upset.

Low.label: The Round-and-Round
summaries: You talk it all out, then talk it out again.

You care about getting to the bottom of things, so you talk, and talk, and circle back. Feelings come first for you, and that’s fair, but the conversation can loop before it lands anywhere. When a plan does come, it sometimes fades within a week.
behaviors: You can spend two hours on a fight and still not know what changes tomorrow.
You hear the complaint and mean to change, but old habits sneak back.
You need to feel understood before you can think about solutions.
strengths: You never brush a problem off. You take it seriously.
weaknesses: Talking about the problem can start to feel like solving it. It isn’t.
realLife: On a first date: You fall into the great filter coffee or chai debate and enjoy it for an hour without a winner.
In a fight: You’ve said the same thing three different ways. Stop and ask: “What’s one thing we could try?”
tips: Give each fight two halves: twenty minutes to feel, ten to fix. Set a timer if it helps. The second half is where things change.
match: Best with: Someone warm who lets you feel it, then gently nudges toward a plan.
Green flag: They say “I get it” first and “so what do we do?” second.
Careful with: Someone who jumps straight to fixes and leaves you feeling unheard.

VeryLow.label: The Daily Soap
summaries: Same fight, new episode, dramatic music.

You feel fights fully, and you need the feeling heard before anything else can happen. So the same argument comes back, episode after episode, with flashbacks to who said what. It isn’t that you love drama. Nobody, you included, has stopped long enough to ask what the real problem is.
behaviors: The dishes fight has run for more seasons than your favourite serial.
In a fight, “who started it” feels more urgent than “what now”.
You make up warmly, and the same topic is back next week.
strengths: You feel things honestly and never pretend a problem doesn’t matter.
weaknesses: Going over who said what can keep you both from ever reaching what’s next.
realLife: On a first date: You both go to different cafés with the same name. Half the date is a funny replay of whose fault it was.
In a fight: You’re on episode five of the same fight. Ask: “What would make this one the last?”
tips: End every fight with one small plan: who does what, starting when. Write it down if you have to. Even a tiny plan breaks the rerun.
match: Best with: Someone patient and practical who listens first, then suggests a small fix.
Green flag: They ask “what would actually help?” and wait for your answer.
Careful with: Someone who enjoys the drama too, so the episodes never end.

Undecided.label: The Feel-Then-Fix Type

You need a few minutes to let the feelings out, and then you’re ready to think. You’re good at finding a fix once the heat is gone, though the fixes don’t always stick. Some fights you solve, some you just survive, and you can tell which is which.

You come up with plans that work, for a few weeks at least.
When a fight repeats, you notice it on the third round, not the first.
strengths: You can go from upset to useful in one conversation.
weaknesses: Your plans can fade once the fight does.
realLife: On a first date: The café you picked is shut. You grumble for a minute, then find a better one round the corner.
In a fight: You need five minutes of “I can’t believe this”, and then you’re the one with an idea.
tips: When you make a plan, set a check-in: “Let’s see how it’s going in two weeks.” Plans that get checked on tend to stick.
match: Best with: Someone who gives you room to vent and then helps you build a plan.
Green flag: They remember the plan you made and check in on it, kindly.
Careful with: Someone who wants a solution before you’ve finished being upset.

tests.title: Forgiveness
tests.subtitle: Let go vs keep score
tests.description: Measures whether you can forgive and move forward or keep score and punish.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your ability to let go after repair.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Forgiveness predicts long-term peace; score-keeping predicts slow relationship death.

questions.text: They forgot your birthday, then apologised properly and made it up to you. Six months later…

options.text: It still stings a little on birthdays
It comes up in every fight we have
It’s forgiven, and honestly forgotten

questions.text: “I forgive, but I don’t forget.” That’s…

options.text: Not me. Forgiving means letting it go
Exactly me

questions.text: A college friend who once said something mean about you wants to catch up over coffee. You…

options.text: Reply politely, but don’t meet
Go. People change, and so do I
Leave them on read. Some things don’t undo
Go, but stay a bit guarded

questions.text: They apologised properly for yesterday’s fight. Today, you’re…

options.text: Polite, but cool. They should feel it a bit
Back to normal: memes, teasing, all of it
Mostly fine, just a bit quieter than usual

questions.text: A new small fight about weekend plans. In your head, you’re…

options.text: Quietly adding it to the list
Only thinking about this weekend
Remembering last time, but not saying it
Linking it to last month’s fight

questions.text: At a cousin’s wedding, an aunt who was rude to your parents years ago greets you warmly. You…

options.text: Smile and keep it short
Give her the coldest namaste of her life
Hug her back. It was years ago

questions.text: Your flatmate broke your favourite mug, said sorry and bought you a new one. You…

options.text: Still bring it up when they borrow anything
Use the new one happily. Done
Mention the old mug now and then, as a joke

questions.text: A colleague took credit for your work last year, then apologised. Now they need your help. You…

options.text: Help, but keep an eye on my credit this time
“Sorry, swamped.” Let them feel it
Help them. That was last year

tests.measures: whether you can let go after repair or keep score

VeryHigh.label: The Fresh-Start Soul
summaries: Every sunrise, a fresh page.

You don’t do grudges. Holding on feels heavier to you than any hurt, so you let it go and mean it, often before the other person has finished saying sorry. People feel lighter around you, because with you, nobody is defined by their worst day.
behaviors: You forgive fast and fully, and you never bring it up again.
Even the rude aunt at a family wedding gets a warm hug from you.
You believe people can change, and you give them room to.
strengths: Your heart never gets weighed down by old stuff.
weaknesses: Forgiving too fast can let the same hurt happen again and again.
realLife: On a first date: They spill a drink on you and panic. You laugh and say it’s already forgotten, because it is.
In a fight: You’re ready to move on before the fight is even over. Make sure the problem got fixed too.
tips: Forgive freely, but keep one rule: if the same hurt comes back three times, it isn’t a mistake anymore. Say so, kindly and clearly.
match: Best with: Someone who respects your soft heart and never takes it for granted.
Green flag: They change the habit after you forgive, not just say sorry.
Careful with: Someone who keeps hurting you the same way because you always let it go.

High.label: The Blackboard Duster
summaries: Sorry said, lesson learnt, board wiped clean.

Once someone has made it right, you put it down and don’t pick it back up. You don’t keep score, you don’t make people pay, and old fights stay out of new ones. You still remember. You just choose not to carry it.
behaviors: After a sorry, you’re back to teasing them by the next morning.
You never pull an old mistake into a new argument.
Trust comes back fully once they’ve shown they mean it.
strengths: People get to grow around you without their past following them.
weaknesses: You can forgive so smoothly that they miss how much it hurt.
realLife: On a first date: They tell you an embarrassing old story. You laugh with them, and never bring it up again.
In a fight: Even mid-fight, you never say “and last time you…”. Today’s fight is about today.
tips: Before you wipe the board, tell them how much it hurt. Forgiveness lands deeper when they know what it cost you.
match: Best with: Someone who owns their mistakes honestly and doesn’t repeat them.
Green flag: They make it right properly, so letting go feels earned.
Careful with: Someone who keeps making the same mistake because they know you’ll forgive.

Moderate.label: The Yellow-Card Type
summaries: First foul, a warning. Second foul, a proper talk.

You forgive easily when someone means it, and you really do move on. But you also learn: the second time, you watch a little closer. Small things go fast, big things take time, and you don’t pretend otherwise.
behaviors: After a real sorry, you’re back to normal, just a bit quieter for a day.
You forgive the mistake, and keep an eye on whether it repeats.
You don’t bring up old fights, though you remember the big ones.
strengths: You give people a real chance without handing them a blank cheque.
weaknesses: Your quiet watching can feel like a test they don’t know they’re taking.
realLife: On a first date: They’re late, apologise sweetly, and you let it go. If date two starts late too, you’ll notice.
In a fight: You keep it to today’s issue, but the big old stuff is quietly in the room.
tips: If you’re watching for a repeat, say so: “I’m giving this another go, and it matters to me.” A clear chance is easier to keep.
match: Best with: Someone who keeps their word, so second chances are rarely needed.
Green flag: They treat your second chance as a gift, not a right.
Careful with: Someone who counts on your forgiveness and never changes.

Low.label: The Forgive-Not-Forget Type
summaries: Forgiven, yes. Forgotten? Let’s not get carried away.

You do forgive. You’re not one to hold a grudge forever. But you keep a copy, just in case, and it can slip out in a new fight or a little joke. Letting go completely feels risky to you, like dropping your guard.
behaviors: You accept the sorry, and the memory stays on file.
An old hurt can come back as a joke, a sigh or a look.
After a big mistake, trust comes back slowly, step by step.
strengths: You forgive, and you learn. You don’t walk into the same wall twice.
weaknesses: A small reminder now and then can feel like a life sentence to them.
realLife: On a first date: They admit they once ghosted someone. You laugh, and you remember.
In a fight: That old thing is on the tip of your tongue. Keep it there. Today’s fight is enough.
tips: When an old hurt comes up in your head, ask: “Has this been made right?” If yes, let the thought pass without saying it.
match: Best with: Someone patient who rebuilds trust with steady actions, not speeches.
Green flag: They show change over time, without asking you to forget overnight.
Careful with: Someone who demands you “just move on” the day after they hurt you.

VeryLow.label: The Ledger Keeper
summaries: Every hurt is noted, dated and filed.

You remember everything: the forgotten birthday, the rude aunt, the exact words from three fights ago. It isn’t pettiness, it’s protection: being hurt twice by the same thing scares you more than holding on. The trouble is, a full ledger gets heavy, and you carry it everywhere.
behaviors: In a new fight, old entries come out as evidence.
Even after a sorry, you need them to feel it for a while.
You forgive slowly, and you rarely forget.
strengths: You spot patterns early and never get fooled twice.
weaknesses: If nothing is ever fully closed, they may stop trying to make things right.
realLife: On a first date: They mention being late to their own sister’s wedding. You laugh, and you make a note.
In a fight: The old files are open. Pick only today’s problem, and close the drawer on the rest.
tips: When someone truly makes it right, close the entry out loud: “Okay, that one’s done.” Then never reopen it. Every closed page makes you lighter.
match: Best with: Someone consistent and honest who gives the ledger very little to write.
Green flag: They make real changes, not just apologies, so the entries stop coming.
Careful with: Someone who says sorry often but never changes, so the ledger keeps growing.

Undecided.label: The Yellow-Card Type
summaries: First foul, a warning. Second foul, a proper talk.

You forgive easily when someone means it, and you really do move on. But you also learn: the second time, you watch a little closer. Small things go fast, big things take time, and you don’t pretend otherwise.
behaviors: After a real sorry, you’re back to normal, just a bit quieter for a day.
You forgive the mistake, and keep an eye on whether it repeats.
You don’t bring up old fights, though you remember the big ones.
strengths: You give people a real chance without handing them a blank cheque.
weaknesses: Your quiet watching can feel like a test they don’t know they’re taking.
realLife: On a first date: They’re late, apologise sweetly, and you let it go. If date two starts late too, you’ll notice.
In a fight: You keep it to today’s issue, but the big old stuff is quietly in the room.
tips: If you’re watching for a repeat, say so: “I’m giving this another go, and it matters to me.” A clear chance is easier to keep.
match: Best with: Someone who keeps their word, so second chances are rarely needed.
Green flag: They treat your second chance as a gift, not a right.
Careful with: Someone who counts on your forgiveness and never changes.

tests.title: Security
tests.subtitle: Trust level & reassurance needs
tests.description: Shows how secure you feel in romance and how easily jealousy is triggered.
tests.whatYouLearn: Whether you stay calm in uncertainty or get triggered by small cues.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Helps avoid insecurity loops by matching reassurance level and trust style.

questions.text: They’re out with their office team tonight and say they’ll be home late. You…

options.text: Keep checking if they’re online on WhatsApp
Say “have fun!” and order Swiggy for one

Feel sure something’s off and stay up till they’re back

“Lucky them. Good friends are rare”

options.text: “Busy day. They’ll reply when they can”
Back to my message, looking for what I said wrong
Straight to “they’ve lost interest”
“Hmm, odd”, and then back to my evening

questions.text: Something they said at dinner stung a little. On the way home you…

options.text: Wait a day to see if it still matters
Tell them simply: “That stung a bit”
Go quiet to see how long they take to notice
Drop hints until they ask what’s wrong

options.text: Spend the evening imagining what “something” is
Feel flat, but wait for the explanation
Reply “No worries, hope all’s okay at home”
Reply “okay.” and feel a bit hurt

options.text: Join in and be my usual warm self
Find a reason to pull them away, fast
Go get pani puri. They’re allowed to talk
Watch from across the room, a little tight inside

questions.text: Deep down, when someone loves you, it feels…

options.text: Mostly safe, a bit wobbly on bad days
Like it could end any day, so I stay alert
Safe. They chose me, and they keep choosing me
Good, but I try not to get used to it

questions.text: A year in, a small doubt about them creeps in. What do you do with it?

options.text: Say it, no blame: “I felt a bit left out today”
Ask for proof: their phone, their plans, everything
Sit with it and see if it passes
Keep it in, till it leaks out as taunts

tests.measures: how secure you feel in relationships and how easily jealousy is triggered

VeryHigh.label: The Calm Harbour
summaries: Nothing rattles your sense of being loved.

You feel secure in love from the inside out. You don’t check, test or keep score, because your sense of worth doesn’t hang on anyone’s reply time. It isn’t coldness. It’s a deep, quiet steadiness that lets the people you love feel free and safe at the same time.
behaviors: Their close friends become your friends, not your rivals.
You never need to see their phone to know where you stand.
Your calm helps even a worried person slowly relax.
strengths: You’re a safe place. People feel trusted with you, so they open up.
weaknesses: You may forget that others need reassurance you don’t, and read their worry as fuss.
realLife: On a first date: You’re fully present and curious about them, and not once checking how it’s going.
In a fight: You stay steady, ask what’s really going on, and never use their fears against them.
tips: Not everyone grew up with your kind of calm. Say the reassuring thing out loud now and then, even when it feels obvious to you.
match: Best with: Someone who wants a calm, grown-up kind of love, or a worrier ready to learn what safe feels like.
Green flag: They match your openness: plans shared, feelings named, no games.
Careful with: Someone who tries to make you jealous just to get a reaction.

High.label: The Sunny Truster
summaries: You assume the best, and you’re usually right.

You give trust first and ask questions only when something real comes up. Late replies, nights out, old friendships: none of it feels like a threat, because you know what you bring to the table. People relax around you, and that makes them want to stay.
behaviors: You enjoy hearing about their night out instead of worrying through it.
A slow reply means a busy day to you, nothing more.
When something does feel off, you ask once, calmly, and believe the answer.
strengths: You make people feel trusted, and trusted people tend to rise to it.
weaknesses: You might miss a real pattern because you always pick the kindest explanation.
realLife: On a first date: They take a work call halfway through. You sip your coffee and people-watch, totally fine.
In a fight: You talk about the actual problem, not about whether they still love you.
tips: Keep the trust, and keep your eyes open too. If the same thing bothers you three times, it deserves a calm, direct talk.
match: Best with: Someone with their own full life, who loves coming home to your calm.
Green flag: They’re as open with you as you are generous with them.
Careful with: Someone who takes your easy trust as permission to be careless.

Moderate.label: The Honest Wobbler
summaries: Calm most days, and honest about the shaky ones.

You trust by default, but you’re human: a cancelled plan or a flirty stranger can still pinch. What sets you apart is that you know your wobbles and don’t make them anyone else’s job. You feel it, name it, and get on with your evening.
behaviors: Most late replies don’t bother you. One on a bad day might.
You’ll say “okay, that made me a bit jealous” and laugh about it later.
You need a little reassurance sometimes, and you ask for it plainly.
strengths: You’re honest about your feelings without turning them into blame.
weaknesses: On a low day, small things can feel bigger than they are, and you may not see why.
realLife: On a first date: You’re relaxed and fun. When they mention their ex once, you notice it, and let it go.
In a fight: You say what bothered you in one line, hear them out, and it’s done within the hour.
tips: Notice what your wobbles have in common: tired days, certain people, long silences. Knowing your pattern turns it from a mystery into a plan.
match: Best with: Someone open and easygoing, who takes a “that bugged me” in their stride.
Green flag: They listen when you say something pinched, without getting defensive.
Careful with: Someone who calls every honest feeling “drama”.

Low.label: The Light Sleeper
summaries: You trust, with one ear always open.

You want to trust, and most days you do. But a part of you never fully switches off, ready in case things go wrong, because being caught off guard once was enough. You rarely make a scene. You just feel the wobble inside and carry it quietly.
behaviors: You believe their words, and still relax more once you see the plan.
A sudden change in their routine stays on your mind for days.
You need to hear “we’re good” a little more often than you admit.
strengths: You’re loyal and alert, and you can tell when something truly needs a talk.
weaknesses: You keep small worries to yourself until they grow bigger than they were.
realLife: On a first date: You have a lovely time, then replay their goodbye all the way home: was that warm enough?
In a fight: You go quiet and watchful. Say the worry while it’s still small and easy to fix.
tips: Say small worries out loud while they’re small: “Hey, that made me a bit unsure.” One easy sentence now saves one big talk later.
match: Best with: Someone warm and predictable, who doesn’t mind saying the sweet stuff out loud.
Green flag: They check in without being asked, especially on their busy days.
Careful with: Someone vague about plans who gets irritated by simple questions.

VeryLow.label: The Midnight Overthinker
summaries: You love hard, and your mind keeps watch all night.

You feel everything at full volume, and love is the loudest of all. Somewhere along the way you learnt that good things can slip away, so your mind keeps watch: a late reply, a new name, a shorter text. It isn’t a lack of love. It’s a lot of love with nowhere calm to rest.
behaviors: A slow reply can turn into a whole story in your head by 1 am.
You notice everything: a new follower, a changed DP, a missing emoji.
When you finally feel safe, you’re the most devoted person in the room.
strengths: You notice the smallest change in someone, and you never take love for granted.
weaknesses: Your worries can start asking for proof that nobody could ever fully give.
realLife: On a first date: You arrive early, check your phone twice, then relax the moment they laugh at your joke.
In a fight: You want it fixed tonight. Start with “I’m scared, not angry”: it lands softer than a list of questions.
tips: When a 1 am story starts, write it down and read it again at breakfast. Most night-time stories don’t survive daylight. Ask calmly about the ones that do.
match: Best with: Someone steady and patient, who says “I’m here” without being asked twice.
Green flag: They tell you their plans before you ask, and they keep them.
Careful with: Someone who enjoys keeping you guessing, or jokes about your worries.

Green flag: They listen when you say something pinched, without getting defensive.
Careful with: Someone who calls every honest feeling “drama”.

tests.subtitle: Do you compare yourself to others

tests.whatYouLearn: Whether jealousy comes from external comparisons.

tests.measures: how much you compare yourself to others and how it affects jealousy

VeryHigh.label: The Underrated Gem
summaries: Everyone sees your shine except you.

You feel deeply, notice everyone, and often end up feeling like the least impressive person in the room. Somewhere you learnt that love has to be earned by being the best, so a perfect couple online or a charming stranger can make you feel replaceable. You aren’t. You just haven’t heard it enough to believe it.
behaviors: An attractive person near them can make you feel invisible in a second.
You may fear they’ll find someone “better” even when they’re clearly all in.
When you do feel chosen, you love with your whole heart and then some.
strengths: You’re humble and kind, and you never take someone’s love for granted.
weaknesses: Your mind ranks you lower than anyone who loves you ever would.
realLife: On a first date: You spend ten minutes sure they’re out of your league, and the next two hours proving yourself wrong.
In a fight: You may hear “I’m upset” as “I’m leaving”. Breathe, and ask what they actually need.
tips: For one month, mute the accounts that leave you feeling small. Notice how you feel at the end. Your feed should cheer for you, not grade you.
match: Best with: Someone patient and warm who chooses you out loud, again and again.
Green flag: They introduce you with pride and make you feel like the only one in the room.
Careful with: Someone who keeps you unsure on purpose, or praises others to make you try harder.

High.label: The Hard Grader
summaries: You mark yourself harder than anyone else ever would.

You have high standards, and the first person you hold to them is you. Seeing someone smarter, better-looking or more settled can quietly convince you that you’re falling behind. It comes from wanting to be worth loving, which is exactly what you already are.
behaviors: Their good-looking colleague can stay on your mind longer than you’d like.
You sometimes wonder what they see in you, even when it’s obvious.
Compliments help, but you tend to argue with them.
strengths: You keep growing. Your drive to be better makes you a thoughtful person to love.
weaknesses: You compare your everyday self to other people’s best photos.
realLife: On a first date: You change outfits three times, then forget all about it once they start laughing with you.
In a fight: You can hear “you did this wrong” as “you’re not enough”. Check which one they actually said.
tips: Every night this week, write down one thing you did well. Small, specific, yours. It slowly teaches your inner grader to give marks too.
match: Best with: Someone generous with praise who says specific things: “I love how you handled that.”
Green flag: They tell you what they like about you, without you having to fish for it.
Careful with: Someone who praises other people’s looks and never yours.

Moderate.label: The Inspired Observer
summaries: You compare sometimes, and turn it into fuel.

You do look around: at a batchmate’s promotion, a cousin’s wedding, the couples on your feed. Sometimes it pinches, but more often it pushes you to try harder at the gym, at work, or in love. You’re learning which comparisons help you grow and which just steal your sleep.
behaviors: You notice attractive people around them, and feel it for a moment.
Someone’s sweet anniversary post might become your next date idea.
A rough day can make you ask “am I enough?”, and you know to say it out loud.
strengths: You turn envy into ambition more often than not.
weaknesses: Some days you compare your inside to everyone else’s outside, and lose.
realLife: On a first date: You admire their style, then quietly add a new shirt to your cart that night.
In a fight: If you feel compared, you say it: “It sounds like I’m not enough.” That gets the real talk going.
tips: When a comparison stings, ask yourself: “Do I want their life, or just one thing in it?” Then go after that one thing.
match: Best with: Someone encouraging, who notices your progress and not just your results.
Green flag: They make you feel chosen, not just lucky to be there.
Careful with: Someone who uses other people to push you: “Why can’t you be more like them?”

Low.label: The Quick Shrugger
summaries: You notice, you shrug, you move on.

You’re human, so a gorgeous colleague or a shiny engagement shoot registers for a second. Then you shrug and get back to your own life, which you actually like. You’ve learnt that comparing is a game with no winners, and you mostly skip it.
behaviors: A glance at their attractive colleague’s profile, and then you’re done.
You can hear about their exes without keeping a scorecard.
On rare low days, you might need a little extra “you’re the one”.
strengths: You bounce back fast. One scroll can’t ruin your evening.
weaknesses: You sometimes shrug off feelings that deserve a moment of attention.
realLife: On a first date: They’re more stylish than you expected. You enjoy it instead of feeling underdressed.
In a fight: You keep it to what happened, and you don’t drag anyone else into it.
tips: On the days a comparison does sting, say so: “Silly, but that got to me.” Saying it out loud takes away most of its power.
match: Best with: Someone secure and warm, who makes you laugh when you overthink.
Green flag: They’re proud of you in public, not only in private.
Careful with: Someone who mentions how good-looking other people are a little too often.

VeryLow.label: The One and Only
summaries: You don’t compete. You’re busy being you.

You measure your life with your own ruler, not anyone else’s. Gorgeous exes, rich cousins and perfect couples online barely register, because you know nobody else is running your race. It isn’t arrogance. It’s a settled sense that there’s only one you, and that’s plenty.
behaviors: Their ex’s photos don’t interest you. Their present does.
You can compliment someone attractive in front of them and mean it.
You never ask “am I better than them?”, because the question doesn’t occur to you.
strengths: You’re hard to shake. Your confidence doesn’t need anyone else to lose.
weaknesses: You may not get why someone else worries about being compared, and brush it off too fast.
realLife: On a first date: They mention their very impressive ex. You ask one curious question and move happily on.
In a fight: You argue about the issue, never about who’s more of a catch.
tips: If someone you love does compare themselves, don’t say “that’s silly”. Tell them what you see in them. Your certainty can lend them some.
match: Best with: Someone who loves you for exactly who you are and never plays “who’s better”.
Green flag: They celebrate other people’s wins, the way you do.
Careful with: Someone who keeps comparing you to others, even as a joke.

Let it go, but feel funny about it all morning

tests.measures: how much digital behavior (social media, texts, follows) triggers jealousy

VeryHigh.label: The Blue-Tick Reader
summaries: Every like, view and ‘last seen’ lands in your heart.

For you, the phone is where love shows up or goes missing. A story watched without a reply, a stranger in the likes, a late ‘last seen’: each one can hurt for real, because you care so much and want to feel sure. It isn’t silliness. It’s a big heart with a very sensitive screen.
behaviors: A late-night ‘online’ can keep you awake, wondering who they’re talking to.
Being posted, tagged and replied to makes you feel chosen.
You may want their passwords, or their ex gone, just to feel safe.
strengths: You care, visibly. Nobody you love ever feels ignored by you.
weaknesses: Your phone can show you a hundred clues and still miss the person in front of you.
realLife: On a first date: You’ve seen their whole profile, back to 2016. Let them tell you the stories anyway.
In a fight: You may lead with “who is this?”. Try “I got scared when I saw this” instead.
tips: Try one week of not checking their likes or ‘last seen’. Notice how your evenings feel. Then tell them what you need, in words.
match: Best with: Someone patient and openly affectionate, online and off, who doesn’t mind saying where things stand.
Green flag: They tell you about awkward online moments before you could find them.
Careful with: Someone who plays games online to make you jealous.

High.label: The Pattern Spotter
summaries: You read the online signals fast, and feel them deeply.

You notice who they follow, when they’re online and who keeps liking their posts, often before they do. For you, how someone behaves online says something about their heart. You want openness, because guessing hurts more than knowing.
behaviors: You feel closer when they post you, and you notice when they don’t.
A new name in their likes can stay on your mind for a while.
Clear online habits, like no secret chats, help you relax completely.
strengths: You’re perceptive. You often pick up on real problems early.
weaknesses: Not every pattern is a message. Sometimes a like is just a thumb.
realLife: On a first date: You know their dog’s name before they mention it, and you act surprised.
In a fight: You come with screenshots in your head. Lead with the feeling instead: “I felt left out.”
tips: Talk early about what feels okay online for you both. One clear talk beats a month of quiet watching.
match: Best with: Someone open and steady online, who’s happy to talk about what you both feel okay with.
Green flag: They’re proud to be seen with you, online and off.
Careful with: Someone with a hidden account, or who flirts in DMs and calls it nothing.

Moderate.label: The Sometimes Sleuth
summaries: You notice online clues, then solve them with a question.

You’re not paranoid, but you’re not blind either. A new follow, a 2 am ‘last seen’, an ex in the likes: you notice, and sometimes it nags at you. The good part is that you’d rather ask than spend the night investigating.
behaviors: You like a little openness online, like a story together once in a while.
Odd online details make you curious, and you ask about them lightly.
On a low day, a like from the wrong person can sting more than it should.
strengths: You catch things early and talk about them before they grow.
weaknesses: On tired days, a small clue can turn into a big theory.
realLife: On a first date: Their phone pings once. You notice, decide it’s nothing, and get back to the momos.
In a fight: You bring up the online thing as a question, not as evidence.
tips: Make one rule for yourself: no investigating after midnight. If it still matters in the morning, ask.
match: Best with: Someone who’s naturally open about their phone and their people.
Green flag: They answer online questions easily, without getting defensive.
Careful with: Someone who gets angry the moment you ask about anything online.

Low.label: The Chill Scroller
summaries: You see it, you scroll past it.

You’re online like everyone else, and sometimes a like or a new follow catches your eye. But you rarely build a story out of it. You know most of the internet is just people being bored, and you treat it that way.
behaviors: You might notice their ex liking a post, and you mostly let it go.
You enjoy a couple photo, but you won’t ask for one.
If something online really bothers you, you ask once and believe the answer.
strengths: You keep online noise in its place, so your relationship stays about the two of you.
weaknesses: Sometimes you let something slide that you’d actually like to talk about.
realLife: On a first date: You glance at their profile once, then forget it and just enjoy the evening.
In a fight: You keep it about what happened between you, not about who liked what.
tips: When a small online thing sticks for more than a day, mention it lightly. A small thing said beats a small thing saved up.
match: Best with: Someone open about their online life, without making it a big deal.
Green flag: They mention things before you could ever wonder: “My ex messaged, I didn’t reply.”
Careful with: Someone secretive about one particular chat or account.

VeryLow.label: The Offline Soul
summaries: Love lives in real life for you, not in likes.

You see social media as noise: fun sometimes, but never a mirror of anyone’s heart. You don’t count likes, study follows or decode ‘last seen’, and you’d honestly forget your own password. Your calm comes from what happens face to face, over chai, not on a screen.
behaviors: You won’t notice who they followed this week, and wouldn’t care if you did.
A couple photo on their grid is sweet, but never a test.
You’d rather they look up from their phone than post about you.
strengths: Nothing online can start a fight in your head. Your peace is offline and solid.
weaknesses: You may miss that online gestures matter a lot to someone else, and seem careless.
realLife: On a first date: You didn’t check their profile beforehand, so every story they tell is new to you.
In a fight: If they bring up something online, you listen, even if it seems small to you.
tips: If the person you love cares about posts and stories, a small public gesture costs you nothing and tells them a lot.
match: Best with: Someone who also lives more off the screen than on it.
Green flag: They put the phone face down when they’re with you.
Careful with: Someone whose whole mood depends on how a post performs.

tests.subtitle: Control vs trust

tests.whatYouLearn: Your control impulse under insecurity.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Prevents toxic dynamics by predicting boundary and control tendencies.

tests.measures: how controlling or possessive you become in relationships

VeryHigh.label: The Open Palm
summaries: Love held in an open hand, never a fist.

You believe the people who love you will stay, and the ones who won’t were never yours to keep. So you don’t check, limit or keep tabs. You give freedom the way other people give gifts, and being loved by you feels like breathing out.
behaviors: You cheer the loudest when they go on a trip without you.
You never make a rule where a conversation will do.
Their friends, all of them, are welcome in your life.
strengths: You make people feel free and trusted, which is the most attractive thing there is.
weaknesses: You can be so relaxed that someone who needs a little reassurance feels unseen.
realLife: On a first date: They say their best friend is also their ex. You ask how they stayed close, and mean it.
In a fight: You never ask them to give anything up. You ask what’s going on, and you listen.
tips: Freedom is your gift, but some people also need to hear that you’d miss them. Say it out loud, even when you know they’ll come back.
match: Best with: Someone secure and independent who doesn’t need to be watched to stay loyal.
Green flag: They choose you openly, every day, with nothing to hide.
Careful with: Someone who wants you to be jealous as proof that you care.

High.label: The Light Touch
summaries: You care a lot, and hold it lightly.

You’d rather someone stay because they want to than because they have to. You enjoy their friends, their trips and their nights out, and you trust them to come home happy. Jealousy visits you sometimes, but it never gets to drive.
behaviors: Their office party is their fun. You’ll hear the gossip later.
You never ask for their location, and they love you for it.
When something does bother you, you say it plainly and move on.
strengths: With you, people feel free, so they choose you again and again.
weaknesses: You may play it so cool that they wonder whether you’d even mind.
realLife: On a first date: They chat happily with the waiter, the auto driver and the couple at the next table. You find it adorable.
In a fight: You talk about what happened, not about who is allowed to do what.
tips: Let them see you care, now and then. A small “I missed you tonight” tells them your calm isn’t distance.
match: Best with: Someone independent who also loves coming back to you at the end of the day.
Green flag: They respect your freedom as much as you respect theirs.
Careful with: Someone who reads your relaxed love as permission not to try.

Moderate.label: The Kite Flyer
summaries: You give them the whole sky, and keep a hand on the string.

You believe in freedom, and mostly live it: trips with their gang, office parties, plans of their own. Now and then a flicker of jealousy wants a bit more string, and you notice it. You’ve learnt to feel it without acting on every pull, which is a real skill.
behaviors: You say “go, have fun” and mean it, even if you’d like a text later.
A charming stranger near them gets a glance from you, not a scene.
You like a few clear basics and leave the rest to trust.
strengths: You can feel jealous and still act fair. Most people can’t do both.
weaknesses: On a bad day, you can tug the string a little harder than you meant to.
realLife: On a first date: They mention a trip with their gang next month. You say “sounds fun” and only slightly wish you were going.
In a fight: You admit the jealous bit honestly, then talk about what you actually need.
tips: When you feel the pull, wait ten minutes before acting on it. Most tugs pass. The ones that don’t are worth a calm talk.
match: Best with: Someone with their own life who still makes you feel like their favourite person.
Green flag: They come back from their plans happy to tell you everything.
Careful with: Someone who hides small things to avoid a scene you were never going to make.

Low.label: The Bear Hug
summaries: Warm, protective, and sometimes a little too tight.

You’re the one who drops them home, remembers their big meetings and wants to know they reached safely. Most of the time it’s pure care. But when you feel unsure, care can slide into checking and questions, and you feel yourself wanting more control than you’d like.
behaviors: You like knowing their plans, and feel uneasy when you don’t.
A night out without you is fine, as long as you hear from them.
You’re generous with your time, and quietly hope for the same back.
strengths: People feel looked after with you. You make love feel safe and warm.
weaknesses: Your care can start to sound like questions they have to answer.
realLife: On a first date: You insist on dropping them home, and text “reached?” ten minutes later.
In a fight: You may fire off a lot of questions at once. Ask the one that matters most, then listen.
tips: Before you ask for an update, ask yourself: is this for their safety or for my worry? If it’s worry, say that instead. It’s more honest, and it lands softer.
match: Best with: Someone who loves being looked after and tells you kindly when it’s too much.
Green flag: They check in on their own and include you in their plans.
Careful with: Someone who gets secretive about ordinary plans.

VeryLow.label: The Hold-Tight Heart
summaries: You love like you’re scared to lose it, because you are.

When you love someone, you love with your whole chest, and the fear of losing them is just as big. So you hold on tight: you want to know where they are, who they’re with, and that you still come first. It comes from love and fear, not from wanting power. But to the person you’re holding, it can start to feel like a cage.
behaviors: You’d happily spend every free evening together, and hope they would too.
Their plans without you can leave you feeling left behind.
You show love by showing up for everything, and you want the same back.
strengths: Your loyalty is total. When you’re in, you’re all in, and you show up every time.
weaknesses: Holding too tight can squeeze the very love you’re scared to lose.
realLife: On a first date: You’re fully present and charming, and you’ve planned the second date before the bill comes.
In a fight: You want promises, right now. Ask for a hug and a talk first. Promises made in fear rarely last.
tips: When you feel the urge to make a rule, say the fear instead: “I’m scared of losing you.” Fear shared brings people closer. Rules push them away.
match: Best with: Someone warm and steady who reassures you often, and still keeps their own friends and plans.
Green flag: They tell you where they are because they want to, not because you asked.
Careful with: Someone who makes you jealous on purpose, or drops their whole life for you in week two.

Undecided.label: The Kite Flyer

You like a few clear basics and leave the rest to trust.

Careful with: Someone who hides small things to avoid a scene you were never going to make.

tests.title: Trust Rebuild
tests.subtitle: How you recover after doubts
tests.description: Measures your ability to rebuild trust after mistakes, misunderstandings, or past betrayal.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your flexibility in rebuilding trust vs staying guarded forever.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Helps predict if the couple can recover after mistakes or will stay stuck.

questions.text: They told a small lie about Saturday to dodge a fight, then owned up and said sorry. You…

options.text: Can’t stop wondering what else they lie about
Forgive, and keep a closer eye for a while
Accept it, and ask them to just tell me next time
Need a few days of distance before I can talk

questions.text: Months after a big fight you both sorted out, you’re arguing about something else. Does the old one come up?

options.text: Only if it’s really connected
Yes. It’s part of a pattern
No. Settled is settled
Not out loud, but I’m thinking it

questions.text: When someone you love hurts you, what can actually win your trust back?

options.text: Honestly, nothing. Once it breaks, it breaks
Seeing them change, slowly, over time

questions.text: After a fight, they’re trying hard: chai in bed, extra calls, little surprises. You…

options.text: Accept it, but remind them of what they did
Let it soften me. They’re clearly trying
Appreciate it, and wait to see if it lasts
Stay cold. A few cups of chai don’t fix it

questions.text: Your closest friend told the group something you’d shared in confidence. They apologised. A month later…

options.text: We’re fine, but I share less with them now
I’ve dropped them. That was it
We’re close again. One mistake isn’t the whole person
We’re polite, but it’s never been the same

questions.text: You were sure they were hiding something. It turned out to be a surprise party for you. Afterwards you…

options.text: Wonder what else they can hide this well
Laugh at myself and trust them a little more
Feel silly, and still notice I’m a bit watchful

questions.text: After a real mistake, what do you need before you can trust them again?

options.text: A real sorry, and a change I can see
Time. Lots of it
Full access to their phone for a while
Proof, again and again, for months

questions.text: Your flatmate paid back a loan late, with a real apology. Now they need to borrow again. You…

options.text: Lend it. They did keep their word in the end
Lend a smaller amount
Say no. Once was enough
Lend it, with a little lecture about last time

tests.measures: how quickly you rebuild trust after it's been damaged

VeryHigh.label: The Fresh Page
summaries: Where others see a burnt bridge, you see something to rebuild.

You believe most hurts can be repaired when both people want it, and you’re willing to do your half. You can talk about pain without wanting revenge, and once something is truly settled, it stays settled. This isn’t naivety. It’s a strong, warm heart that knows people are more than their worst moment.
behaviors: A real apology lands with you, and the matter is closed.
You never throw an old fight back at them in a new one.
After a misunderstanding, you’re the first to say “let’s start fresh”.
strengths: You make people feel they can be human with you, mistakes included.
weaknesses: You can forgive so easily that someone stops trying, or keeps repeating the same hurt.
realLife: On a first date: They admit they nearly cancelled out of nerves. You laugh, and like them more for saying it.
In a fight: You calm things down, talk about the hurt, and mean it when you say it’s over.
tips: Your forgiveness is a gift, so give it to people who change. If the same hurt keeps coming back, walking away is also a kind of repair.
match: Best with: Someone just as willing to repair, who respects your forgiveness instead of counting on it.
Green flag: They work to rebuild trust without being asked, and they keep it up.
Careful with: Someone who treats your forgiveness as a free pass. Your kindness deserves effort back.

High.label: The Rebuilder
summaries: Real effort gets a real second chance from you.

You know that good people still mess up, and that what they do next matters more than the mistake. When someone owns it and changes, you let the hurt go and move forward with them. Grudges feel heavy to you, and you’d rather travel light.
behaviors: After a fight, you’re back to normal once things are truly sorted.
You notice effort, and you let it reach you.
You don’t keep a list of past mistakes to use later.
strengths: You make repair possible. With you, a bad day doesn’t have to be the end.
weaknesses: Sometimes you forgive the words before the change has actually shown up.
realLife: On a first date: A clumsy start doesn’t bother you. You’d rather see how they recover.
In a fight: You fight to fix it, not to win, and you make up properly afterwards.
tips: Forgive freely, and still watch the pattern. A second chance is a gift; a fifth one for the same thing is a habit.
match: Best with: Someone honest who owns their mistakes and grows from them.
Green flag: They apologise specifically: what they did, why it hurt, what they’ll change.
Careful with: Someone who keeps needing the same second chance.

Moderate.label: The Careful Mender
summaries: You fix what’s torn, stitch by stitch, eyes open.

You believe in second chances, and in watching what happens next. When someone hurts you, you don’t cut them off, and you don’t pretend it didn’t happen. You forgive in steps, trusting a little more each time they show up right.
behaviors: You forgive a real mistake, and keep an eye out for a while.
You’d rather talk it through than punish them with silence.
You need both words and actions before things feel normal again.
strengths: You balance kindness and caution. People get a fair chance with you.
weaknesses: Watching for too long can make the other person feel on permanent probation.
realLife: On a first date: They arrive late but own it right away. That earns them more points than being on time.
In a fight: You say what hurt, ask what will be different, and give them time to show it.
tips: Decide what ‘trust rebuilt’ looks like for you, like a few months of easy honesty. When you get there, let yourself relax for real.
match: Best with: Someone who takes responsibility easily and doesn’t mind earning trust back.
Green flag: They make amends without being asked twice.
Careful with: Someone who apologises beautifully and changes nothing.

Low.label: The Slow Thaw
summaries: You can forgive, but it takes a long winter.

You don’t slam doors, but a hurt freezes something in you, and it thaws slowly. You need to see change many times before you believe it. Part of you keeps a small file of what happened, just in case, because your heart wants proof before it opens again.
behaviors: After a fight, you’re polite long before you’re warm again.
A sorry helps, but steady weeks of good behaviour help more.
Old hurts can slip into a new argument when you’re tired.
strengths: When you do trust again, it’s real and solid, not a quick patch.
weaknesses: Bringing up old hurts can keep you both stuck in the same fight.
realLife: On a first date: You’re warm but careful, and you notice every promise they make, even the small ones.
In a fight: You may reach for an old example. Keep it to today’s problem, and you’ll both be heard.
tips: When you forgive something, say it out loud: “That one’s closed.” Then try not to reopen it. It frees you as much as them.
match: Best with: Someone patient and consistent, who doesn’t rush your healing or give up on it.
Green flag: They keep showing up the same way long after the apology.
Careful with: Someone who says “you should be over it by now”.

VeryLow.label: The Locked Vault
summaries: Your trust is precious, and once lost, it stays locked.

You don’t hand out trust easily, and when someone breaks it, the door closes with a click. It isn’t coldness. You take loyalty seriously, and you’ve probably learnt the hard way that people don’t always change. Protecting yourself became a habit. It has kept you safe, and sometimes lonely.
behaviors: One lie, even a small one, can change how you see someone for good.
Apologies make you more watchful, not less.
When someone does keep your trust, you’re loyal for life.
strengths: Your loyalty means something. People know your trust is earned, not handed out.
weaknesses: You may close the door on people who were truly ready to change.
realLife: On a first date: You notice whether they arrive when they said they would, and you remember.
In a fight: You go quiet and close off. Try saying “I need time” instead of “we’re done”.
tips: Next time someone sincerely says sorry, give them one small chance to show it before you shut the door. Let what they do next decide, not what others did before.
match: Best with: Someone consistent and honest from day one, who never makes you wonder.
Green flag: They own small mistakes quickly, before you even notice them.
Careful with: Someone who brushes off small lies as “no big deal”.

Green flag: They make amends without being asked twice.
Careful with: Someone who apologises beautifully and changes nothing.

tests.subtitle: What calms you down
tests.description: Measures what kind of reassurance you need: words, actions, transparency, time, affection.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your calming inputs when jealousy appears.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Helps match partners who can reassure in the right language.

options.text: Believe them, but the thought pops back later

options.text: A few days, till the next small thing
For good. It’s sorted
Till the end of the call
A few hours, then I need to hear it again

options.text: A promise, and I lean on it
Words. People say that

options.text: Feel heard. It’s gone
Feel their sorry was just to end the talk
Say it’s fine, but replay the party all week
Feel better once they plan a day just for us

options.text: Is fine. That text was plenty
Is mostly fine, with a peek at my phone now and then
Goes into rereading “love you” for hidden meaning

options.text: Hug back, still running the scene in my head
Melt. That’s all I needed
Feel better, but still want to talk it through
Feel they’re dodging the question

options.text: Say “No need, I believe you”
Read every line, and ask about the emojis
Take a quick look, then feel silly and relieved
Read it all, and still feel unsure

questions.text: Diwali night. They’re at their family’s, replying slowly, then send a selfie: “Miss you.” You…

options.text: Wonder why it took them so long
Heart it and enjoy my own family chaos
Feel warm, and want a call later anyway

tests.measures: how well reassurance calms you when jealousy or doubt shows up

VeryHigh.label: The Easy Exhale
summaries: One honest answer, and your shoulders drop.

Doubt doesn’t stick to you. When you feel a flicker of jealousy, you ask, hear the answer and actually let it go. You take people at their word because you trust yourself to handle it if they ever break it. That makes you wonderfully easy to love, and easy to be honest with.
behaviors: You don’t need to see the chat. Their offer to show you is enough.
A quick “love you, busy day” keeps you happy till evening.
After a talk, you’re back to normal by dinner, not next week.
strengths: You let peace happen. Small worries pass through you without leaving a mark.
weaknesses: Not everyone settles as fast as you, and you may rush someone who needs longer.
realLife: On a first date: They say they’ll text when they reach home. You fall asleep before it comes, smiling.
In a fight: You hear them out, take the apology, and the fight is over. Completely.
tips: When someone you love needs more reassurance than you do, give it generously. What settles you in a minute may take them a day, and that’s okay.
match: Best with: Someone honest and warm, who never gives you a reason to doubt their word.
Green flag: They tell you things before you need to ask.
Careful with: Someone who takes your easy trust for granted and stops explaining at all.

High.label: The Warm-Word Believer
summaries: Say it kindly once, and you believe it.

When someone you love explains, you listen, and then you let it go. You give people the dignity of being believed. Doubt still visits sometimes, but a clear word, an open answer or a warm hug sends it on its way quickly.
behaviors: One “sorry, phone died” is enough. You don’t need the story twice.
A small affectionate message can carry you through a busy day.
You ask straight when something bothers you, and accept a straight answer.
strengths: You make reassurance easy. People feel believed with you, so they stay honest.
weaknesses: You might accept a vague answer once too often because you like believing people.
realLife: On a first date: They say they had a great time. You believe them, and you sleep like a baby.
In a fight: Once they explain and apologise, you’re genuinely done. No reruns.
tips: Keep believing people, and notice when a story changes. Trust works best with your eyes open.
match: Best with: Someone honest and direct who says what they mean.
Green flag: Their words and their actions match, week after week.
Careful with: Someone whose explanations keep changing.

Moderate.label: The Top-Up Type
summaries: A little reassurance, now and then, keeps you full.

Most days you feel secure, and you don’t need much to stay that way. But like a phone battery, you run a bit low after a busy week or a strange evening, and a warm word or a long hug tops you right up. You know this about yourself, which helps a lot.
behaviors: A warm text in the middle of the day goes a long way with you.
You can take an explanation and let it go, most of the time.
On wobbly days, you ask for a little extra and feel fine after.
strengths: You know what you need, and you can ask for it simply.
weaknesses: You might wait till you’re running on empty before asking for a top-up.
realLife: On a first date: A “had fun tonight” text afterwards is all you need to sleep happy.
In a fight: A hug and one clear sentence, “we’re fine”, settle you quickly.
tips: Ask early, while you’re at half battery: “Can I get a hug? Long day.” Small asks keep you from big worries.
match: Best with: Someone affectionate in small ways, who enjoys checking in.
Green flag: They notice when you’re a bit low and offer a hug before you ask.
Careful with: Someone who calls a small need for reassurance “clingy”.

Low.label: The Gentle Doubter
summaries: Reassurance helps you, just not all in one go.

You want to believe, and usually you do, eventually. A first explanation calms you a bit; the second, a day later, does the rest. You’re not difficult, you’re thorough: your heart likes to hear the same truth twice before it fully relaxes.
behaviors: You’ll accept their explanation, then ask one more question the next day.
Steady actions calm you more than big speeches.
A hug helps your body relax, while your mind takes a little longer.
strengths: Once you’re truly reassured, your trust is solid and deep.
weaknesses: Asking again can sound like you don’t believe them, even when you do.
realLife: On a first date: You enjoy it, then text the next morning just to hear it went well for them too.
In a fight: You need a clear ending. Ask for one, “So, are we good now?”, and then believe the yes.
tips: Tell them early: “Sometimes I need to hear it twice. It’s not distrust, it’s how I settle.” It turns your second ask into something they understand.
match: Best with: Someone patient who doesn’t mind saying it twice, kindly.
Green flag: They answer your second question as warmly as your first.
Careful with: Someone who gets defensive at simple questions.

VeryLow.label: The Restless Ocean
summaries: Your worries come in waves, even on calm days.

You feel things deeply, and doubt doesn’t leave just because someone explains. Even when the facts are good, a wave of worry can roll back in an hour later. It isn’t that you don’t believe them. Some part of you learnt that calm can be a trick, and it’s still on duty.
behaviors: You may ask “are we okay?” again even after a lovely evening.
Kind words help for a while, then the worry finds its way back.
Even seeing their chats may not settle you, and that frustrates you too.
strengths: You never take love lightly. You feel every bit of it, the good included.
weaknesses: When no answer is ever enough, the person trying to reassure you can start to feel helpless.
realLife: On a first date: It goes well, and you still read their goodbye text three times to be sure.
In a fight: You may keep circling back. Try asking yourself: “What would help me let this go tonight?”
tips: When the worry comes back, wait twenty minutes before asking again. Ride the wave out. Each wave you ride out makes the next one a little smaller.
match: Best with: Someone patient and steady, whose actions stay the same week after week.
Green flag: They stay calm when you ask again, without getting irritated.
Careful with: Someone who goes hot and cold. Mixed signals feed your waves.

Undecided.label: The Top-Up Type

Most days you feel secure, and you don’t need much to stay that way. But like a phone battery, you run a bit low after a busy week or a strange evening, and a warm word or a long hug tops you right up. You know this about yourself, which helps a lot.

You can take an explanation and let it go, most of the time.
On wobbly days, you ask for a little extra and feel fine after.

In a fight: A hug and one clear sentence, “we’re fine”, settle you quickly.

Careful with: Someone who calls a small need for reassurance “clingy”.

tests.title: Boundary Respect
tests.subtitle: Healthy boundaries with others
tests.description: Measures whether you can respect boundaries (friends, privacy, time) without turning it into jealousy drama.
tests.whatYouLearn: Your boundary maturity under insecurity.
tests.howItHelpsMatch: Matches improve when both respect boundaries and communicate them clearly.
